title: Gravitational waves
one_line_summary: Builds gravitational waves by replaying the electromagnetic gauge-theory argument with one extra index: vacuum plane waves of the trace-reversed perturbation, transverse-traceless gauge and the + and x polarizations read off from geodesic deviation of a ring of test masses, a conservation-law argument that gravity radiates first at quadrupole order, the Einstein quadrupole formula and the quadrupole luminosity, binary inspiral and the Hulse-Taylor pulsar, an exact plane-wave check in light-cone coordinates, and the interferometric detection of GW150914 with a survey of future detectors.
role_in_book: Chapter 45 linearized the Einstein equation and, in Lorenz gauge, reduced it to a sourced wave equation; this chapter cashes that in. It sits in Part VI because the whole treatment is framed as field theory: Chapter 42's electromagnetic potentials, gauge freedom and retarded solutions supply the template, and each step for light is repeated for the metric perturbation. Geodesic deviation (Chapters 11 and 35) turns the abstract solution into measurable tidal motion, and the energy-momentum tensor of Chapter 12 underlies the radiated-power calculation. The chapter closes the classical account of gravitational radiation and hands over to Chapter 47, which quantizes the same waves into gravitons and explains the spin-2 character hinted at by the 45-degree polarization rotation.

learning_objectives: Reader can reproduce the electromagnetic chain (Lorenz gauge, wave equation, Coulomb gauge, transverse polarization vectors) and say which step gains an index in gravity.
Reader can substitute a plane-wave ansatz into the vacuum wave equation and Lorenz condition to derive k.k = 0 and k^mu A_{mu nu} = 0, and interpret them as propagation at c and transversality.
Reader can use a residual gauge transformation with d^2 xi = 0 to impose tracelessness and A_{mu nu}u^nu = 0, reaching transverse-traceless gauge and the 2x2 amplitude matrix with two free entries.
Reader can explain why a free test mass keeps fixed TT coordinates while the proper distance to a neighbour oscillates, and compute that oscillation to first order in the amplitude.
Reader can derive the relative accelerations of test masses from geodesic deviation with weak-field Riemann components, and draw the + and x deformation patterns of a ring of particles.
Reader can explain why the two gravitational polarizations are 45 degrees apart while electromagnetic ones are 90 degrees apart, linking this to the rank of the field.
Reader can argue from conservation of mass, momentum and angular momentum that gravitational radiation has no monopole or dipole part and starts at quadrupole order.
Reader can state the Einstein quadrupole formula, estimate the strain from a stellar-mass binary at 100 Mpc (about 1e-21), and explain the role of retarded time.
Reader can explain why gravitational-wave energy is only defined after averaging over several wavelengths, and quote the effective stress-energy t_{mu nu} in TT gauge.
Reader can state the quadrupole luminosity L = (G/5c^5)<dddot I_ij dddot I_ij>, apply it to an equal-mass circular binary, and derive the period decay dP/dt.
Reader can explain why a bound binary speeds up (spin-up) as it radiates, and connect this to the Hulse-Taylor pulsar timing data.
Reader can set up the light-cone metric -du dv + F(u)^2 dx^2 + G(u)^2 dy^2, obtain the vacuum condition F''/F + G''/G = 0, and recognize the linearized + wave inside it.
Reader can explain how a Michelson interferometer converts h_+ into a phase difference proportional to arm length, and why LIGO needs km arms and Fabry-Perot cavities.
Reader can place ground interferometers, LISA, pulsar timing arrays and the primordial background on the gravitational-wave frequency spectrum.

teaching_approach.summary: An analogy-first, derivation-heavy chapter that treats gravity as a second gauge field. Every move is first rehearsed for electromagnetism (gauge fixing, plane waves, polarization) and then repeated for the metric perturbation, with the extra index being the recurring source of novelty. Physical meaning is extracted operationally from the motion of free test masses, with a deliberately staged false start (the coordinate of a mass does not move) to teach coordinate suspicion. Formal results are carried mostly in boxed Examples; heavy algebra (Isaacson stress-energy, TT projection, the conservation-law route to the quadrupole formula) is pushed to exercises. The second half pivots to order-of-magnitude astrophysics and a descriptive survey of detection.
narrative_arc: Motivate with history: prediction, the 1993 and 2017 Nobel prizes, and the promise of describing LIGO.
Rehearse electromagnetism: sourceless wave equation, Lorenz gauge, plane waves, Coulomb gauge leaving two transverse polarizations.
Replay for gravity: Lorenz-gauge wave equation for hbar, plane-wave ansatz, constraints k.k=0 and transversality; margin argument that the wave rides with a light ray.

Exhaust the residual gauge freedom with an oscillatory xi to reach transverse-traceless gauge; write the amplitude matrix and the oscillating line element; split into two polarizations related by 45 degrees.
Stage a paradox: a single test mass does not move in these coordinates; resolve it with proper distance between two masses.

Use geodesic deviation with weak-field Riemann components to get relative accelerations, integrate to the displacement formula, and draw the ring-of-masses and acceleration-field pictures; define the tidal field and polarization tensors.
Ask what sources can radiate: multipole expansion for electromagnetism, then conservation laws killing gravitational monopole and dipole terms.

Solve the sourced equation with retarded Green's function, apply the compact-source limit and energy-momentum conservation to reach the Einstein quadrupole formula; estimate the strain for a black-hole binary.
Confront the smallness of h and the problem of defining wave energy: background split, second-order Einstein tensor, averaging to get t_{mu nu}.
Derive radiated power by flux through a large sphere and angular integration; obtain quadrupole luminosity and angular-momentum loss.

Apply to an equal-mass Newtonian binary: luminosity, energy-period relation, period decay; connect to Hulse-Taylor spin-up; warn that Newtonian and linear assumptions fail at merger and that gravity is nonlinear.
Show waves survive nonlinearity with an exact plane-wave metric in light-cone coordinates, recovering the + polarization at small amplitude.

Describe detection: Michelson geometry, phase shift proportional to arm length times strain, LIGO parameters, GW150914; survey ET, Cosmic Explorer, LISA, pulsar timing arrays and the primordial background; point ahead to gravitons.
signature_moves: Parallel-derivation pedagogy: the gravitational argument is literally a rerun of the electromagnetic one with square matrices replacing column vectors.
Deliberate dead end ('the particle doesn't move') used to teach that coordinate values in a chosen gauge carry no physics, followed by the proper-distance rescue.
Physical meaning of polarization given by deformations of a circle of free masses and by quadrupole-magnet-like acceleration field lines.
Radiation selection rules argued from conservation laws (charge for EM; mass, momentum, angular momentum for gravity) rather than from a full multipole calculation.
Immediate numerical sanity checks after each formula (strain 5e-21, luminosity 1e47 W, Earth potential 1e-9) to give scale.
Heavy but standard algebra (Isaacson average, TT projector, conservation identities for the quadrupole formula) outsourced to long guided exercises.
Short exact-solution section to reassure that the linear picture is not an artefact, done with light-cone coordinates and a two-function metric.
Ends with a narrative survey of experiments and a forward pointer to the quantum (graviton) view.

sections.title: Chapter opening: prediction, prizes and plan
sections.summary: A Shakespeare epigraph about waves opens a short historical framing: the waves were anticipated by Poincare and predicted by Einstein, earned indirect support from the Hulse-Taylor binary pulsar (1993 Nobel) and direct detection by LIGO (2017 Nobel to Weiss, Thorne and Barish). The plan is to review electromagnetic waves first and then repeat the reasoning for a weak gravitational field.
key_moves: Announce the electromagnetism-first strategy.
Anchor the topic in the two Nobel prizes to motivate the observational finale.

sections.title: Waves in a gauge theory
sections.summary: Starts from the sourceless Maxwell equation for the potential, fixes Lorenz gauge to obtain a plain wave equation with plane-wave solutions, then uses the leftover freedom (a gauge function obeying the wave equation) to also set A^0 = 0. The Coulomb condition makes k perpendicular to the polarization vector, leaving two transverse linear polarizations along x and y for a wave moving along z. The same steps are then applied to the trace-reversed metric perturbation: the Lorenz condition gives the vacuum wave equation, a plane-wave ansatz with a symmetric amplitude matrix is inserted, and the two constraints k.k = 0 and k^mu A_{mu nu} = 0 follow. A margin argument shows the wave phase is constant along a light ray, so the wave moves with light. The section ends by writing the surviving components as functions of t - z and flagging that a further gauge choice should remove the time components.

null wavevector and propagation at the speed of light
key_moves: Lorenz gauge removes the divergence term in eqn 46.1, leaving d^2 A = 0 (46.2).
Residual shift by a function with d^2 xi = 0 allows A_0 = 0; div A = 0 then gives k.epsilon = 0 (46.4).
Count: four potential components, two physical polarizations (46.6).
Gravity: Lorenz condition on hbar gives d^2 hbar = 0 (46.8); polarizations become matrices.
Insert hbar = Re[A e^{ik.x}] to get i k^nu A_{mu nu} = 0 and k.k = 0 (46.10-46.12).
Light ray x = k lambda + l keeps k.x constant (46.13-46.14), so phase surfaces move with light.

sections.title: Lorenz gauge for gravitational waves
sections.summary: Uses the residual gauge freedom x -> x + xi with d^2 xi = 0 and an oscillatory xi = B e^{ik.x} to shift the amplitude by terms built from B and k while preserving transversality; B is chosen to make the amplitude traceless and orthogonal to a chosen 4-velocity, which defines transverse-traceless gauge (where h = hbar). In the rest frame of u with the wave along z only A_xx = -A_yy and A_xy survive, giving an oscillating line element that splits into two plane waves related by a 45 degree rotation. A test mass at rest keeps constant coordinates because Gamma^i_00 vanishes, but the proper distance to a second mass oscillates with fractional amplitude A_xx/2. Geodesic deviation with the weak-field Riemann tensor yields relative accelerations proportional to second time derivatives of h, integrating to a displacement of half h_ij times the separation, which produces the + and x ring deformations of Fig. 46.1 and the quadrupolar acceleration fields of Fig. 46.2; the tidal field E_ij = R_0i0j and polarization tensors e_+, e_x are defined.

TT coordinates of free test masses
45 degree polarization rotation and field rank
key_moves: Residual gauge with d^2 xi = 0 (46.16) and xi = B e^{ik.x} shifts A by -i(B k + k B - eta B.k) (46.19).
Choose B so A^alpha_alpha = 0 and A u = 0 (46.20): transverse-traceless gauge.
In the u rest frame with k along z, A has only A_xx = -A_yy and A_xy (46.21); line element 46.22 splits into 46.23 and 46.24.
Geodesic equation gives zero coordinate acceleration (46.25): the 'oh dear' moment.
Proper length integral gives L + (L A_xx/2) cos(omega t - kz) (46.26).
Geodesic deviation with u = (1,0,0,0) and R_{x0x0} = -(1/2) d_t^2 h_xx etc. (46.28-46.30) gives relative accelerations (46.31-46.32).

Define E_ij = R_0i0j = -(1/2) ddot h^TT_ij and e_+, e_x (46.34-46.36).

sections.title: 46.2 (cont.) Example 46.8: multipoles and why gravity radiates at quadrupole order
sections.summary: A boxed detour compares sources. For electromagnetism, a bounded charge distribution is expanded into monopole, dipole, quadrupole and magnetic moments; charge conservation freezes the monopole, so antennas radiate by oscillating a dipole. For gravity, the mass monopole is fixed by mass conservation, the mass dipole (centre of mass) by momentum conservation, and the current dipole (angular momentum) by angular-momentum conservation, so the lowest radiating multipole is the mass quadrupole. Expansions of g_00 in mass moments and g_0j in current moments, with dimensional scaling I_l ~ M L^l and S_l ~ M v L^l, support the claim that the mass quadrupole dominates the time-varying field.
concepts: absence of monopole and dipole gravitational radiation
key_moves: Charge conservation forbids electromagnetic monopole radiation; dipole is the leading term.
Mass, momentum and angular-momentum conservation freeze the three lowest gravitational moments.
Metric expansions 46.37-46.38 plus scaling show the mass quadrupole is the leading time-dependent term.

sections.title: Quadrupolar radiation
sections.summary: Restores the source and G in the linearized equation and writes the retarded Green's-function solution by direct analogy with the electromagnetic retarded potential. For a compact source far away the spatial components reduce to an integral of T_ij at retarded time; energy-momentum conservation converts this into the second time derivative of the second mass moment, giving the Einstein quadrupole formula hbar_ij = (2G/R) ddot I_ij(t - R). The moment of inertia tensor differs from the quadrupole moment only by its trace, which the TT description ignores. A numerical estimate for two 30 solar-mass black holes at 100 Mpc gives a strain of a few times 1e-21. The section then notes that such tiny, rapidly varying ripples ride on a curved background, that the split between background and wave is ambiguous, and that the waves carry energy that itself gravitates; this is modelled by moving the quadratic part of the Einstein tensor to the source side and averaging over several wavelengths and periods to get a meaningful effective stress-energy t_{mu nu}.
concepts: retarded solution of the linearized field equation
second mass moment and reduced quadrupole moment
effective energy-momentum tensor of gravitational waves
key_moves: Retarded solution 46.41 copied from the electromagnetic version 46.40.
Compact source at distance R: pull 1/R out and evaluate at t - R (46.42).
Use d_mu T^{mu nu} = 0 (Exercise 46.3) to trade the integral of T_ij for (1/2) d_t^2 of the integral of y_i y_j T^00 (46.43).
Name the result the Einstein quadrupole formula (46.44, with c restored in 46.45).
Estimate |hbar| ~ 32 pi^2 G M a^2 f^2/(c^4 R) ~ 5e-21 (46.46).
Compare with the Earth's |h_00| ~ 1e-9; introduce g = g^b + h (46.47).
Move G^(2) to the right-hand side as t_{mu nu} (46.48-46.51); average to restore gauge invariance (46.52).

sections.title: Radiated energy and power
sections.summary: Quotes the averaged stress-energy in TT gauge (derived in Exercise 46.2), inserts the quadrupole formula to get the energy density in terms of third time derivatives of I_ij, and computes the power as flux through a large sphere using energy-momentum conservation and the divergence theorem. Because the field depends on t - R/c, the radial flux equals the energy density. An identity for the TT part of a traceless tensor plus angular averages of products of unit vectors (Exercise 46.5) gives the quadrupole luminosity G/(5c^5) times the averaged square of the third derivative of I_ij, with an extremely small prefactor. The black-hole binary of the previous example radiates about 1e47 W but delivers under a milliwatt per square metre at Earth. An analogous flux integral gives the angular-momentum loss rate.
concepts: effective energy-momentum tensor of gravitational waves
energy flux through a distant sphere
angular momentum carried by gravitational waves

Energy conservation plus divergence theorem gives dE/dt as a surface integral (46.55-46.56).
Outgoing wave: d_r hbar = -d_0 hbar, so t^{0r} = t^{00} (46.57).
dE/dt = (G/8 pi c^5) integral <dddot I^TT dddot I^TT> dOmega (46.58).
TT identity (46.59) and angular integrals yield L = (G/5c^5)<dddot I_ij dddot I_ij> (46.60).
Numbers for the binary: L ~ 1e47 W (46.61).
Angular momentum flux (46.62) gives dJ/dt = (2G/5c^5) eps_ijk <ddot I_jl dddot I_kl> (46.63).

sections.title: 46.4 (cont.) Binary inspiral, spin-up and the Hulse-Taylor pulsar
sections.summary: For two equal Newtonian masses in a circular orbit, the virial energy E = -GM^2/(4a) and Kepler's law convert the luminosity into a function of separation (proportional to 1/a^5) and the energy into a function of period, so that the period derivative follows. Since the bound energy is negative, radiating makes |E| larger, shrinks the orbit and shortens the period: the orbit speeds up. This is tied to the Hulse-Taylor pulsar (59 ms pulsar, 7.75 h orbit, period falling by roughly 76.5 microseconds per year) and Fig. 46.3. The angular-momentum loss is computed both from the radiation formula and from the orbital relation between E and J, and the two agree. The subsection warns that Newtonian dynamics and linearization fail near merger, and contrasts electromagnetism (uncharged photons, linear in vacuum) with gravity (waves carry energy that gravitates, so the theory is nonlinear).
concepts: binary inspiral driven by gravitational radiation
angular momentum carried by gravitational waves
key_moves: Newtonian circular orbit: omega^2 = GM/(4a^3), E = -GM^2/(4a) = -M a^2 omega^2 (46.64).
E proportional to P^{-2/3} (46.66), so dP/dt = -(3/2)(P/E) dE/dt (46.67), giving 46.68.
Negative E means losing energy speeds up the orbit; compare Hulse-Taylor data.
dJ_z/dt from eqn 46.63 (46.69) equals the result from E = -G^2 M^5/(4J^2) (46.70).

sections.title: An exact solution
sections.summary: Asks whether waves survive in the full nonlinear theory. Introduces light-cone coordinates u = t - z and v = t + z, takes a metric -du dv + F(u)^2 dx^2 + G(u)^2 dy^2, lists its nonzero connection coefficients and Riemann components, and finds the vacuum Einstein equation reduces to F''/F + G''/G = 0. Setting F = 1 + epsilon and G = 1 - epsilon satisfies it for small epsilon and reproduces the + polarized wave, which the authors take as evidence that wave solutions persist beyond linear order.
key_moves: Minkowski metric in null coordinates: ds^2 = -du dv + dx^2 + dy^2 (46.71).
Ansatz with two profile functions of u only (46.72).
Riemann components -F''/F and -G''/G (46.74) give the single vacuum condition 46.75.
Small-amplitude check with F = 1 + eps, G = 1 - eps (46.76) recovers h_xx = -h_yy = eps.

sections.title: The discovery of gravitational waves
sections.summary: Describes ground-based detection in the 10 Hz to 10 kHz band dominated by compact binary coalescences. Free mirrors along two perpendicular arms of a Michelson interferometer register the + pattern; strains of order 1e-21 demand that light stay in the arms for about half a gravitational-wave period (milliseconds), hence very long arms. A boxed example relates the output phase to (L_x + L_y) h_+. LIGO's twin 4 km-class detectors with Fabry-Perot arm cavities (effective length about 1200 km) detected GW150914 on 14 September 2015 (roughly 36 and 29 solar masses merging to 62, with 3 solar masses radiated), shown in Fig. 46.5. The section then surveys the Einstein Telescope and Cosmic Explorer, the space-based LISA (100 microhertz to 100 millihertz, massive black-hole binaries), pulsar timing arrays (nanohertz to microhertz, supermassive black-hole remnants) and the primordial stochastic background, and points ahead to gravitons.
concepts: gravitational-wave frequency spectrum and detector bands
key_moves: Map the + ring deformation onto two perpendicular interferometer arms.
Photon storage time must be comparable to half a wave period; arms must be long.
Phase difference Delta phi proportional to (L_x + L_y) h_+ (46.77-46.78): sensitivity grows with arm length.
Fabry-Perot cavities multiply effective optical length; GW150914 masses and energy budget.
Frequency-band survey: ground (10 Hz-10 kHz), LISA (1e-4 to 1e-1 Hz), pulsar timing (nHz-microHz), primordial background.

sections.title: Chapter summary
sections.summary: Five bullets restate the plane-wave form with null wavevector and transverse amplitude, the use of TT gauge to reach the + and x polarizations, the existence of nonlinear wave solutions, the quadrupole luminosity formula, and the growth of gravitational-wave astronomy with LIGO, LISA and pulsar timing arrays.
key_moves: Summary misstates the polarizations as 45 degrees 'out of phase'; they are related by a 45 degree rotation.

concepts.name: gravitational wave
concepts.definition: A propagating, source-free perturbation of the spacetime metric that travels at the speed of light and produces oscillating tidal strains between freely falling masses transverse to its direction of travel.
concepts.how_introduced: Framed historically (Poincare, Einstein, two Nobel prizes) and then derived as the vacuum solution of the linearized Einstein equation in Lorenz gauge, explicitly as the gravitational counterpart of an electromagnetic wave.
prerequisites: linearized vacuum wave equation for hbar

concepts.name: Lorenz gauge
concepts.definition: The gauge condition d_mu A^mu = 0 for the electromagnetic potential, or d^nu hbar_{mu nu} = 0 for the trace-reversed metric perturbation, which reduces the respective field equations to wave equations.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from Chapter 42 as the step that removes the divergence term in the sourceless Maxwell equation, then transplanted to gravity where the analogous condition removes the extra derivative terms of the linearized Einstein tensor.

concepts.name: residual gauge freedom
concepts.definition: The gauge transformations that preserve an already imposed gauge condition; for Lorenz gauge these are shifts generated by functions (EM) or vector fields (gravity) that themselves satisfy the wave equation.
concepts.how_introduced: In electromagnetism a further shift by a function with d^2 xi = 0 keeps Lorenz gauge and allows A_0 = 0; in gravity the coordinate shift xi^mu with d^2 xi_alpha = 0 is used the same way (margin note 10 stresses the extra index).

concepts.name: Coulomb gauge
concepts.definition: The electromagnetic gauge condition div A = 0; in a source-free region combined with A_0 = 0 it leaves only transverse potential components.
concepts.how_introduced: Imposed on top of Lorenz gauge using the residual freedom, making div A = 0 and turning into the transversality condition k.epsilon = 0 for plane waves.

concepts.name: transverse electromagnetic plane wave
concepts.definition: A vacuum solution A = epsilon e^{i k.x} with null k whose polarization vector is perpendicular to the propagation direction, leaving two independent linear polarizations.
concepts.how_introduced: Used as the template: plane waves solve d^2 A = 0, the Coulomb condition gives k.epsilon = 0, and for a wave along z the basis polarizations are unit vectors along x and y.
concepts.notes: Margin note 7 ties the polarization vectors to photon spin states, pointing to Chapter 47.

concepts.name: linearized gravity
concepts.definition: The approximation g = eta + h with |h| << 1 in which the Einstein equation is kept only to first order in h, making it a linear field theory on flat spacetime.
concepts.how_introduced: Assumed from Chapter 45 and used throughout; later the chapter questions its limits (curved background, energy carried by waves, nonlinearity).

concepts.name: trace-reversed metric perturbation
concepts.definition: The combination hbar_{mu nu} = h_{mu nu} - (1/2) eta_{mu nu} h, whose trace is minus that of h; in Lorenz gauge it obeys a simple wave equation, and in TT gauge it coincides with h.
concepts.how_introduced: Carried over from Chapter 45; in TT gauge the tracelessness condition makes the distinction disappear, which the chapter uses to write the line element directly.

concepts.name: linearized vacuum wave equation for hbar
concepts.definition: In Lorenz gauge and away from sources, each component of the trace-reversed perturbation satisfies the flat-space wave equation; with sources the right-hand side is -16 pi G T_{mu nu}.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as looking just like the electromagnetic wave equation but carrying two indices, so polarizations are matrices rather than vectors.

concepts.name: plane gravitational wave ansatz
concepts.definition: A trial solution hbar_{mu nu} = Re[A_{mu nu} e^{i k.x}] with constant symmetric amplitude matrix A and constant wavevector k.
concepts.how_introduced: Written by analogy with the electromagnetic plane wave and substituted into the Lorenz condition and wave equation in Example 46.2.
prerequisites: linearized vacuum wave equation for hbar

concepts.name: null wavevector and propagation at the speed of light
concepts.definition: Plane-wave solutions of the vacuum wave equation require k_mu k^mu = 0, so the wave's phase fronts move at c and are carried along with light rays in the same direction.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained from the wave equation (46.11) and reinforced by margin note 9: a light ray x = k lambda + l keeps k.x constant, so photon and wave share constant-phase surfaces.

concepts.name: transversality condition
concepts.definition: For a plane wave in Lorenz gauge the amplitude contracted with the wavevector vanishes, k^mu A_{mu nu} = 0, so the perturbation has no component along the direction of propagation (once the time components are also removed).
concepts.how_introduced: Derived from the Lorenz gauge condition applied to the ansatz (46.10) and compared to k.epsilon = 0 for light.
concepts.notes: The book writes hbar_{mu z} = 0 already in eqn 46.15, but in Lorenz gauge alone this only fixes A_{alpha z} = -A_{alpha 0}; zero z-components follow after A_{alpha 0} = 0 in TT gauge.

concepts.name: residual gauge transformation in linearized gravity
concepts.definition: An infinitesimal coordinate change generated by a vector field that itself solves the wave equation, taken to oscillate like the wave with constant amplitude B; it alters the wave amplitude by a symmetric combination of B and k (eqn 46.19) without spoiling the Lorenz condition, so its four components can be spent on further simplifications.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 46.3 transforms h and hbar under the shift and shows the new amplitude still satisfies transversality; B is then tuned to impose extra conditions.
formulas: A'_{\alpha\beta} = A_{\alpha\beta} - i(B_\alpha k_\beta + B_\beta k_\alpha - \eta_{\alpha\beta}B^\mu k_\mu)

concepts.name: transverse-traceless gauge
concepts.definition: The gauge in which a gravitational wave's amplitude is traceless, orthogonal to a chosen observer 4-velocity u, and transverse to k; in the observer's frame only spatial components transverse to the propagation direction survive, and h = hbar.
concepts.how_introduced: Reached by choosing the four components of B to impose A^alpha_alpha = 0 and A_{alpha beta}u^beta = 0; Example 46.4 then evaluates it in the rest frame of u with the wave along z.
prerequisites: residual gauge transformation in linearized gravity
concepts.notes: The book does not count constraints explicitly (10 components - 4 Lorenz - 4 residual = 2) or explain why the five conditions in 46.20 are compatible with only four B components.

concepts.name: plus and cross polarizations
concepts.definition: The two independent linear polarization states of a gravitational wave along z: h_+ = h_xx = -h_yy stretches along x while squeezing along y and vice versa, and h_x = h_xy produces the same pattern rotated by 45 degrees.
concepts.how_introduced: Read off from the TT amplitude matrix and line elements 46.23-46.24, then made physical through the ring-of-masses deformations in Fig. 46.1 and the acceleration fields of Fig. 46.2.

concepts.name: TT coordinates of free test masses
concepts.definition: In TT gauge a freely falling particle initially at rest keeps constant spatial coordinates as the wave passes, because Gamma^i_00 vanishes; the coordinates are attached to free masses, so coordinate values alone show no effect.
concepts.how_introduced: Staged as a disappointment in Example 46.5: the geodesic equation gives zero coordinate acceleration, prompting the lesson to distrust coordinates and look at invariant distances.

concepts.name: proper-distance oscillation between test masses
concepts.definition: The physical separation between two free masses a coordinate distance L apart along x oscillates as L[1 + (1/2) h_+ cos(omega t - kz)], giving a fractional length change of half the wave amplitude.
concepts.how_introduced: Computed right after the coordinate paradox by integrating sqrt(g_xx) between the masses; offered as the basis of detection.
prerequisites: TT coordinates of free test masses

concepts.name: geodesic deviation equation
concepts.definition: The relative acceleration of neighbouring geodesics is given by the Riemann tensor acting on the separation vector: D^2 n^mu/dtau^2 = -R^mu_{alpha beta nu} u^alpha n^beta u^nu.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled in index-free form and evaluated in the rest frame of the particles, where only R^mu_{0 alpha 0} matters, to turn the wave metric into measurable tidal accelerations.

concepts.name: weak-field Riemann tensor
concepts.definition: To first order in h, the Riemann tensor is a combination of second derivatives of the metric perturbation and is gauge invariant; for a TT wave the relevant components are R_{i0j0} = -(1/2) d_t^2 h_ij.
concepts.how_introduced: Taken from the previous chapter (46.29) and specialized in Example 46.6 to components R^x_{0x0}, R^y_{0x0}, R^y_{0y0}.

concepts.name: gravitational-wave displacement formula
concepts.definition: A free mass at transverse position x^j relative to a reference mass is displaced by (1/2) h^TT_ij x^j, so displacements are linear in the separation and set by the local TT strain.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by integrating the geodesic-deviation equations 46.31-46.32 twice in time (starting from rest, dropping integration constants), then used to explain Fig. 46.1 and the interferometer phase in Example 46.13.
concepts.notes: The book writes n^i on the left; it is the oscillating change of the separation, not the full separation, and assumes the separation is small compared with the wavelength.

concepts.name: tidal field tensor
aliases: electric part of the Weyl/Riemann tensor
concepts.definition: The spatial tensor E_ij = R_0i0j that gives the relative acceleration of nearby free particles; for a TT wave it equals minus one half of the second time derivative of h^TT.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined in Example 46.7 and decomposed on two polarization tensors to show the wave's tidal action directly.
formulas: \mathcal E = -\tfrac12 \ddot{\mathbf h}^{TT} = -\tfrac12(\ddot h_+ \mathbf e_+ + \ddot h_\times \mathbf e_\times)
concepts.notes: The reading copy renders the dots as an overbar; the printed page has second time derivatives.

concepts.name: polarization tensors
concepts.definition: The basis tensors e_+ = e_x (x) e_x - e_y (x) e_y and e_x = e_x (x) e_y + e_y (x) e_x on the plane transverse to a wave along z; any TT wave is h_+ e_+ + h_x e_x.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced alongside the tidal field as the gravitational analogue of the polarization vectors epsilon_1, epsilon_2 for light.

concepts.name: 45 degree polarization rotation and field rank
concepts.definition: Rotating a gravitational polarization pattern by 45 degrees turns + into x, whereas electromagnetic linear polarizations are related by 90 degrees; the halved angle reflects the rank-2 tensor nature of h compared with the vector (1-form) potential.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated after Fig. 46.1 as a consequence of the (0,2) character of h, with a margin pointer back to the rotation between eqns 46.23 and 46.24.
concepts.notes: The general rule (pattern returns to itself after 180/s degrees for spin s) is not stated; it is the natural bridge to Chapter 47.

concepts.name: quadrupolar acceleration pattern
aliases: tidal field lines of a gravitational wave
concepts.definition: The relative acceleration field of free particles in a passing wave has the shape of a quadrupole: inward along one transverse axis and outward along the perpendicular one, reversing every half period, and rotated by 45 degrees for the x polarization.
concepts.how_introduced: Shown in Fig. 46.2 and likened to the field of a quadrupole magnet, which motivates the question of what sources emit such waves.

concepts.name: multipole expansion of a source
concepts.definition: Representation of the far field of a bounded source as a series of monopole, dipole, quadrupole and higher terms, each weighted by a moment of the source distribution and falling off faster with distance.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 46.8 reviews it for electromagnetism (charge and current moments, antennas as oscillating dipoles) before applying it to masses.

concepts.name: absence of monopole and dipole gravitational radiation
concepts.definition: Because total mass-energy, total momentum (fixing the centre-of-mass dipole) and angular momentum (the current dipole) are conserved for an isolated source, none of these moments can oscillate, so the leading gravitational radiation is quadrupolar.
concepts.how_introduced: Argued in parallel with charge conservation forbidding electromagnetic monopole radiation; margin note 20 adds that a spherically symmetric source has no changing quadrupole and so does not radiate.

concepts.name: mass and current multipole moments
concepts.definition: Moments of the mass density (I_l ~ M L^l) and of the mass current (S_l ~ M v L^l) that control the expansion of g_00 and g_0j far from a source; current moments are suppressed by a factor v relative to mass moments of the same order.
concepts.how_introduced: Written schematically with unspecified constants in eqns 46.37-46.38 and used in a dimensional argument that the time-varying field is dominated by I_2.
formulas: g_{00} = -1 + a_0\frac{\mathcal I_0}{r} + a_1\frac{\mathcal I_1}{r^2} + a_2\frac{\mathcal I_2}{r^3} + \dots

concepts.name: retarded solution of the linearized field equation
concepts.definition: The solution of -d^2 hbar = 16 pi G T that sums contributions of the source at the earlier times from which a light signal could reach the field point: hbar(t, x) = 4G integral T(t - |x - y|, y)/|x - y| d^3y.
concepts.how_introduced: Written by analogy with the electromagnetic retarded potential in margin note 12, repeating the argument of Chapter 45.
prerequisites: linearized vacuum wave equation for hbar
formulas: \bar h_{\mu\nu}(t,\vec x) = 4G\int d^3y\,\frac{T_{\mu\nu}(t - |\vec x - \vec y|,\vec y)}{|\vec x - \vec y|}

concepts.name: retarded time
concepts.definition: The emission time t - R/c at which a source a distance R away must have acted to influence the field at time t, accounting for propagation at the speed of light.
concepts.how_introduced: Appears in the retarded solution and is emphasized after the luminosity and angular-momentum formulas, where the source derivatives are evaluated at t - R/c.

concepts.name: compact-source far-zone approximation
concepts.definition: For a source of size r much smaller than the distance R (and moving slowly), 1/|x - y| can be replaced by 1/R and the retarded time by t - R throughout the source volume.
concepts.how_introduced: Applied to the spatial components to get eqn 46.42 as an integral of T_ij over the source.
prerequisites: retarded solution of the linearized field equation
concepts.notes: The slow-motion condition (source size much smaller than the emitted wavelength) is needed for evaluating all of the source at one retarded time but is not stated.

concepts.name: Einstein quadrupole formula
concepts.definition: Far from a slowly moving compact source, the spatial wave field equals 2G/(c^4 R) times the second time derivative of the source's second mass moment evaluated at the retarded time.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived from the far-zone integral of T_ij by using energy-momentum conservation to rewrite it as (1/2) d_t^2 of the integral of y_i y_j T^00 (worked out in Exercise 46.3), then named and restored with factors of c in margin note 14.
prerequisites: second mass moment and reduced quadrupole moment
concepts.notes: The physical radiation field is the TT projection of this expression; the text glosses this by saying TT gauge is insensitive to the trace.

concepts.name: second mass moment and reduced quadrupole moment
concepts.definition: I_ij is the integral of rho y_i y_j over the source; the reduced (traceless) quadrupole moment Q_ij = I_ij - (1/3) delta_ij Tr I differs only by a trace term, which does not contribute to the TT radiation field.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced just after the quadrupole formula; the book calls I_ij the moment of inertia tensor and notes its trace is irrelevant in TT gauge.
concepts.notes: Not the rigid-body inertia tensor of mechanics, which is the integral of rho(r^2 delta_ij - y_i y_j). The printed Q_ij expression omits delta_ij on the trace term.

concepts.name: conservation of energy-momentum
concepts.definition: In the linearized theory on flat spacetime the matter stress-energy tensor is divergence-free, which links time derivatives of T^00 and T^0i to spatial divergences.
concepts.how_introduced: Used twice: to convert the integral of T_ij into moments of T^00 (Exercise 46.3) and to express energy loss from a volume as a surface flux.

concepts.name: background-plus-ripple decomposition
concepts.definition: Writing the metric as a slowly varying curved background g^b plus a rapidly varying small perturbation h, justified when the wavelength is much shorter than the background curvature scale.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by comparing the wave strain (1e-21) with the Earth's static potential (1e-9) and noting detected wavelengths are short compared with terrestrial scales.
concepts.notes: The book admits the split is ambiguous but does not state the scale-separation criterion that makes it well defined.

concepts.name: effective energy-momentum tensor of gravitational waves
concepts.definition: The averaged second-order part of the Einstein tensor, moved to the source side, that acts as the energy-momentum carried by gravitational waves; in TT gauge it is (c^4/32 pi G) times the average of d_mu h^TT_ab d_nu h^TT_ab.
concepts.how_introduced: Built by expanding G = G^(1) + G^(2) + ..., identifying t = -(1/8 pi)G^(2), noting it is not gauge invariant, and fixing this by averaging over several wavelengths and periods; the TT result is quoted with the derivation left to Exercise 46.2.

concepts.name: non-locality of gravitational field energy
concepts.definition: Gravitational field energy cannot be assigned a meaningful value at a point, because a freely falling frame removes the gravitational field locally; only averages over regions larger than the wave's scale are meaningful.
concepts.how_introduced: Margin note 15 gives the equivalence-principle reason why the unaveraged quadratic Einstein tensor should not be gauge invariant.

concepts.name: averaging over wavelengths
concepts.definition: Averaging a quantity over a spacetime region larger than several wavelengths and periods but smaller than the background curvature scale, which removes gauge-dependent oscillating pieces and allows integrations by parts with vanishing boundary terms.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced to define t_{mu nu}; Exercise 46.2(c) uses its property that total divergences average to zero.

concepts.name: energy flux through a distant sphere
concepts.definition: The power emitted by a source is found by integrating the radial energy flux of the wave, c t^{0r}, over a large sphere of radius R; for an outgoing wave t^{0r} = t^{00}, so power = c R^2 integral t^00 dOmega.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived by differentiating the energy in a volume, using the conservation law and Stokes' (divergence) theorem, then noting that fields depending on t - R/c have radial derivative equal to minus the time derivative.
prerequisites: effective energy-momentum tensor of gravitational waves

concepts.name: transverse-traceless projection operator
concepts.definition: For a propagation direction n, P_ij = delta_ij - n_i n_j projects onto the transverse plane, and M^TT_kl = (P_ik P_jl - (1/2) P_kl P_ij) M_ij extracts the transverse, traceless part of a symmetric tensor.
concepts.how_introduced: Used implicitly in the power calculation through identity 46.59 and constructed step by step in Exercise 46.5, with angular integrals of products of n.

concepts.name: quadrupole luminosity formula
concepts.definition: The total power radiated in gravitational waves by a slowly moving source is G/(5c^5) times the time average of the sum of squares of the third time derivatives of its (traceless) quadrupole moment.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by inserting the field quadrupole formula into t_00, integrating the TT identity over solid angle, and immediately checked for scale: the prefactor G/5c^5 is tiny, so only extreme sources radiate appreciably.
prerequisites: energy flux through a distant sphere
concepts.notes: The angular integral in Exercise 46.5 assumes a traceless tensor, so strictly Q_ij should appear; for sources with constant Tr I (like a circular binary) the results coincide. The reading copy loses a dot; the printed page has third derivatives.

concepts.name: angular momentum carried by gravitational waves
concepts.definition: Gravitational waves remove angular momentum from a source at a rate (2G/5c^5) epsilon_ijk <ddot I_jl dddot I_kl>; an axisymmetric source loses none.
concepts.how_introduced: Set up by analogy with the energy flux integral (46.62), result quoted from Maggiore (46.63), applied to the binary in eqn 46.69 and cross-checked against the orbital E-J relation.

concepts.name: non-radiating symmetric sources
concepts.definition: A source whose quadrupole moment does not change in time, such as a spherically symmetric or steadily rotating axisymmetric body, emits no quadrupole gravitational radiation (and an axisymmetric one emits no angular momentum).
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned in margin notes 20 and 22 as consequences of the luminosity and angular-momentum formulas.

concepts.name: binary inspiral driven by gravitational radiation
concepts.definition: A bound binary loses orbital energy and angular momentum to gravitational waves, so its separation and period shrink over time and its orbital frequency and wave amplitude grow until merger.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 46.11 combines the luminosity for a circular equal-mass Newtonian binary with the energy-period relation to obtain dP/dt, then discusses the limits of Newtonian and linear approximations near merger.

concepts.name: negative binding energy and spin-up
aliases: bound orbits speed up when they lose energy
concepts.definition: The total energy of a gravitationally bound orbit is negative and becomes more negative as the orbit tightens, so removing energy shrinks the orbit and increases orbital speed and frequency.
concepts.how_introduced: Explained after Example 46.11 to justify the minus sign in dP/dt and linked to the Hulse-Taylor observations.

concepts.name: Hulse-Taylor binary pulsar
concepts.definition: A binary of two neutron stars, one seen as a 59 ms radio pulsar, in a 7.75 h eccentric orbit whose period decreases at the rate predicted by gravitational-wave emission, giving the first (indirect) evidence for gravitational radiation.
concepts.how_introduced: Cited as observational confirmation of spin-up, with the cumulative periastron-time shift plotted in Fig. 46.3 against the general-relativity curve.
prerequisites: binary inspiral driven by gravitational radiation
concepts.notes: The book's circular equal-mass formula underestimates the decay rate for this highly eccentric orbit (eccentricity about 0.62) by an order of magnitude; the plotted prediction uses the full elliptical parameters.

concepts.name: nonlinearity of gravity
concepts.definition: Unlike electromagnetic waves, which carry no charge, gravitational waves carry energy and momentum that themselves source curvature, so the full field equations are nonlinear and superposition holds only approximately.
concepts.how_introduced: Raised at the end of the binary discussion and used to motivate checking for exact wave solutions.
prerequisites: effective energy-momentum tensor of gravitational waves

concepts.name: light-cone coordinates
aliases: null coordinates u = t - z, v = t + z
concepts.definition: Coordinates u = t - z and v = t + z adapted to waves moving along plus or minus z, in which the Minkowski line element becomes -du dv + dx^2 + dy^2.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced in Section 46.5 because a wave along +z depends only on u.

concepts.name: exact plane gravitational wave
concepts.definition: An exact vacuum solution ds^2 = -du dv + F(u)^2 dx^2 + G(u)^2 dy^2 whose only nontrivial Einstein equation is F''/F + G''/G = 0; for small deviations from 1 it reduces to a linear + polarized wave.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 46.12 computes connection coefficients and Riemann components for the ansatz and checks the small-amplitude case F = 1 + eps, G = 1 - eps.
concepts.notes: For any chosen F the condition is a linear ODE for G, so exact solutions exist for arbitrary profiles; the book's check is only to first order in eps. Rosen-form coordinates typically develop coordinate singularities as the wave focuses free particles.

concepts.name: laser interferometer gravitational-wave detector
concepts.definition: A Michelson interferometer whose end mirrors are nearly free test masses; a passing wave changes the two arm lengths oppositely by fractions of order h, producing a phase difference at the output proportional to arm length times strain.
concepts.how_introduced: Built from the + polarization picture: masses along x and y form the arms; Example 46.13 derives the phase shift and concludes the arms must be as long as possible, with Fig. 46.4 showing the arm changes.

concepts.name: Fabry-Perot arm cavities
concepts.definition: Partially reflecting mirrors that make light bounce many times along each interferometer arm, multiplying the effective optical path (to about 1200 km in LIGO) and hence the phase response to a strain.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned as LIGO's fix for arms that are still too short, with the requirement that light stay in the arms for about half a gravitational-wave period.

concepts.name: GW150914
concepts.definition: The first directly detected gravitational-wave signal, recorded on 14 September 2015 by both LIGO detectors, produced by the inspiral, merger and ringdown of black holes of about 36 and 29 solar masses leaving a 62 solar-mass remnant and radiating about 3 solar masses of energy.
concepts.how_introduced: Described with its parameters and shown as strain versus time in Fig. 46.5.
prerequisites: binary inspiral driven by gravitational radiation

concepts.name: gravitational-wave frequency spectrum and detector bands
concepts.definition: Different sources dominate different frequencies: stellar-mass compact binaries at 10 Hz-10 kHz (ground interferometers), massive black-hole binaries at 1e-4 to 1e-1 Hz (LISA), supermassive black-hole binaries at nanohertz to microhertz (pulsar timing), and a primordial background extending to about 1e-18 Hz.
concepts.how_introduced: Assembled in the closing survey of current and planned observatories.

concepts.name: pulsar timing array
concepts.definition: A network of millisecond pulsars whose extremely regular pulse arrival times at Earth are monitored for years; a gravitational wave perturbs the arrival times through spacetime changes at the pulsar and at Earth, giving sensitivity at nanohertz to microhertz frequencies.
concepts.how_introduced: Described as the lowest-frequency detection technique, contrasted with laser interferometry.
prerequisites: gravitational-wave frequency spectrum and detector bands

concepts.name: stochastic primordial gravitational-wave background
concepts.definition: A random superposition of gravitational waves produced in the very early Universe, expected to dominate the spectrum at extremely low frequencies and possibly reach bands accessible to current technologies.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned as an open question at the end of the survey.
prerequisites: gravitational-wave frequency spectrum and detector bands

concepts.name: graviton
concepts.definition: The hypothetical force-carrying quantum of the gravitational field, obtained by quantizing gravitational waves, with spin 2.
concepts.how_introduced: Named only as the subject of the next chapter.

concepts.name: gauge transformation
concepts.definition: A change of the field variables that leaves all physics unchanged: A_mu -> A_mu - d_mu chi for electromagnetism, and h_{mu nu} -> h_{mu nu} - xi_{mu,nu} - xi_{nu,mu} under x -> x + xi for linearized gravity.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled at the start of Section 46.1 and applied to the gravitational amplitude in Example 46.3.

key_equations.name: Sourceless Maxwell equation for the potential
key_equations.meaning: The electromagnetic field has its own wave-like dynamics even without charges; margin note 2 adds -J_nu on the right when sources are present.
key_equations.symbols: A_mu 4-potential; d^2 = eta^{mu nu} d_mu d_nu

key_equations.latex: A^t = 0,\ A^x = A^x(-\omega t + |\vec k|z),\ A^y = A^y(-\omega t + |\vec k|z),\ A^z = 0
key_equations.meaning: Only transverse components survive for a wave along z.

key_equations.meaning: Two linear polarizations along x and y, related by a 90 degree rotation.

key_equations.meaning: Reminder of the Lorenz-gauge linearized Einstein equation with matter, in G = 1 units.

key_equations.name: Vacuum gravitational wave equation
key_equations.meaning: Away from sources each component of hbar obeys the flat wave equation; the extra index makes polarizations matrices.

key_equations.name: Plane gravitational wave ansatz
key_equations.meaning: Trial solution with constant symmetric amplitude matrix.

key_equations.meaning: Gauge condition becomes an algebraic constraint on the amplitude.

key_equations.meaning: Transversality of the amplitude and propagation at the speed of light.

key_equations.meaning: Straight null line followed by a photon moving with the wave.

key_equations.name: Constant phase along the ray (margin note 9)
key_equations.meaning: The wave phase does not change along the photon's path, so the wave keeps pace with light.

key_equations.latex: \bar h_{xx},\ \bar h_{xy} = \bar h_{yx},\ \bar h_{yy}\ \text{functions of } (-\omega t + |k|z),\quad \bar h_{\mu z} = 0
key_equations.meaning: Transverse components depend only on the retarded phase.

key_equations.name: Residual gauge condition
key_equations.meaning: Coordinate shifts that keep Lorenz gauge intact.

key_equations.name: Gauge change of h
key_equations.meaning: Linearized effect of x -> x + xi on the metric perturbation.

key_equations.name: Gauge change of hbar
key_equations.meaning: Trace reversal adds the divergence term.

key_equations.name: Gauge change of the amplitude
key_equations.latex: A'_{\alpha\beta} = A_{\alpha\beta} - i\left(B_\alpha k_\beta + B_\beta k_\alpha - \eta_{\alpha\beta}B^\mu k_\mu\right)
key_equations.meaning: With xi = B e^{ik.x} the amplitude shifts by terms built from B and k; transversality is preserved.

key_equations.name: Transverse-traceless conditions
key_equations.meaning: Choice of B making the wave traceless and orthogonal to observer velocity u.

key_equations.name: TT amplitude for a wave along z
key_equations.meaning: Only two independent numbers remain: the two polarizations.

key_equations.name: Line element of a TT plane wave
key_equations.latex: ds^2 = -dt^2 + \left(1 + A_{xx}e^{-i(\omega t - |k|z)}\right)dx^2 + 2A_{xy}e^{-i(\omega t - |k|z)}dx\,dy + \left(1 - A_{xx}e^{-i(\omega t - |k|z)}\right)dy^2 + dz^2
key_equations.meaning: Spatial distances transverse to z oscillate; real part understood.

key_equations.name: Plus-polarized line element
key_equations.latex: ds^2 = -dt^2 + \left(1 + A_{xx}e^{-i(\omega t - |k|z)}\right)dx^2 + \left(1 - A_{xx}e^{-i(\omega t - |k|z)}\right)dy^2 + dz^2
key_equations.meaning: x stretched while y squeezed, and vice versa half a period later.

key_equations.name: Cross-polarized line element
key_equations.meaning: Same physics rotated by 45 degrees. As printed, the dx^2 + dy^2 terms are omitted; with A_xx = 0 the line element should still contain dx^2 + dy^2.

key_equations.name: Geodesic equation for a mass at rest
key_equations.meaning: Since Gamma^i_00 = 0 in TT gauge, the mass keeps fixed coordinates.

key_equations.name: Oscillating proper distance
key_equations.meaning: Physical separation oscillates with fractional amplitude A_xx/2: the measurable effect.

key_equations.name: Geodesic deviation (index-free)
key_equations.meaning: Relative acceleration of neighbouring free particles is set by curvature.

key_equations.name: Geodesic deviation in rest frame
key_equations.meaning: Only the R^mu_{0 alpha 0} components act on particles at rest.

key_equations.name: Linearized Riemann tensor
key_equations.meaning: Curvature to first order in h.

key_equations.name: Riemann components for a TT wave
key_equations.meaning: Tidal components are second time derivatives of the strain.

key_equations.name: Relative acceleration, separation along x
key_equations.meaning: Masses separated along x move along x under h_+ and along y under h_x.
key_equations.symbols: a initial separation; tau = t to first order

key_equations.name: Relative acceleration, separation along y
key_equations.meaning: The y-separated pair responds oppositely to h_+.

key_equations.name: Displacement formula
key_equations.latex: n^i = \tfrac12 h^{TT}_{ij}x^j,\quad h^{TT}_{xx} = -h^{TT}_{yy} = h_+,\ h^{TT}_{xy} = h^{TT}_{yx} = h_\times
key_equations.meaning: Displacement of a free mass relative to the origin is half the strain times its position (the left side is the oscillating change of separation).

key_equations.name: Tidal field of a wave
key_equations.latex: \boldsymbol{\mathcal E} = -\tfrac12\ddot{\mathbf h}^{TT} = -\tfrac12\left(\ddot h_+\mathbf e_+ + \ddot h_\times\mathbf e_\times\right),\quad \mathcal E_{ij} = R_{0i0j}
key_equations.meaning: Tidal tensor expressed through the two polarization amplitudes. The reading copy shows a bar where the printed page has two dots.

key_equations.name: Polarization tensors
key_equations.latex: \mathbf e_+ = \mathbf e_x\otimes\mathbf e_x - \mathbf e_y\otimes\mathbf e_y,\quad \mathbf e_\times = \mathbf e_x\otimes\mathbf e_y + \mathbf e_y\otimes\mathbf e_x
key_equations.meaning: Tensor basis for the two polarizations.

key_equations.name: Mass-moment expansion of g_00
key_equations.latex: g_{00} = -1 + a_0\frac{\mathcal I_0}{r} + a_1\frac{\mathcal I_1}{r^2} + a_2\frac{\mathcal I_2}{r^3} + \dots
key_equations.meaning: Schematic multipole expansion; conserved I_0 and I_1 cannot radiate.
key_equations.symbols: I_l l-th mass moment; a_l constants

key_equations.name: Current-moment expansion of g_0j
key_equations.meaning: Mass-current moments, suppressed by v relative to mass moments.

key_equations.name: Sourced wave equation with G
key_equations.meaning: Starting point for radiation from sources.

key_equations.name: EM retarded potential (margin)
key_equations.latex: A_\mu(t,\vec x) = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int d^3y\,\frac{J_\mu(t - |\vec x - \vec y|,\vec y)}{|\vec x - \vec y|}
key_equations.meaning: Template solution of -d^2 A = mu_0 J.

key_equations.name: Retarded solution for hbar
key_equations.latex: \bar h_{\mu\nu}(t,\vec x) = 4G\int d^3y\,\frac{T_{\mu\nu}(t - |\vec x - \vec y|,\vec y)}{|\vec x - \vec y|}
key_equations.meaning: Field built from the source at retarded times.

key_equations.name: Far-zone spatial components
key_equations.meaning: Compact source at large distance R.

key_equations.name: Conservation-law rewrite
key_equations.meaning: Stress integral traded for the second moment of energy density (Exercise 46.3).

key_equations.name: Einstein quadrupole formula
key_equations.meaning: Wave field set by the second derivative of the source's second mass moment at retarded time.

key_equations.name: Quadrupole formula with c
key_equations.meaning: SI form with I in mass units.

key_equations.meaning: They differ only by a trace, invisible to TT radiation. The printed version omits delta_ij on the trace term.

key_equations.name: Strain estimate for a black-hole binary
key_equations.meaning: For M = 30 solar masses, 2a = 2000 km, f = 10 Hz, R = 100 Mpc; uses ddot I ~ 4 M a^2 omega^2 (the reading copy shows one dot).

key_equations.name: Background plus ripple
key_equations.meaning: Waves ride on a curved slowly varying background.

key_equations.meaning: Dependence on t - R/c equates radial flux and energy density.

key_equations.name: Quadrupole luminosity
key_equations.meaning: Total power radiated; the reading copy loses one dot, the printed page shows third derivatives.

key_equations.name: Luminosity of the black-hole binary
