key_equations.meaning: Surface integral for angular momentum carried off.

key_equations.name: Radiated angular momentum
key_equations.meaning: Rate of angular momentum loss, derivatives at retarded time; zero for axisymmetric sources.

key_equations.name: Orbital frequency of equal-mass binary
key_equations.meaning: Newtonian circular orbit of two masses M at radius a about the centre of mass.

key_equations.name: Luminosity versus separation
key_equations.meaning: Power rises steeply as the orbit shrinks. Here L is the power radiated, so the orbital energy changes at -L.

key_equations.name: Energy versus period
key_equations.meaning: Kepler's law recast for the bound energy.

key_equations.name: Period change from energy change
key_equations.meaning: Logarithmic derivative of E proportional to P^{-2/3}; dE/dt here must be the orbital energy change (negative) for the sign to come out right.

key_equations.name: Orbital period decay
key_equations.meaning: Period shortens (spin-up). A factor 1/c^5 is needed for dimensional consistency in SI units.

key_equations.name: Angular-momentum loss of the binary
key_equations.meaning: From eqn 46.63; equals L/omega as expected for a circular orbit.

key_equations.name: Consistency check from orbital relations
key_equations.meaning: Orbital angular momentum lost equals that carried by waves. The book prints J = sqrt(G M a^3) = -E omega/2, which is dimensionally wrong; the corrected forms are given here.

key_equations.name: Minkowski metric in light-cone coordinates
key_equations.latex: ds^2 = \eta_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu dx^\nu = -du\,dv + dx^2 + dy^2,\quad u = t - z,\ v = t + z
key_equations.meaning: Null coordinates suited to waves along z.

key_equations.name: Exact plane-wave ansatz
key_equations.meaning: Two profile functions of the null coordinate u.

key_equations.name: Connection coefficients of the ansatz
key_equations.meaning: Nonzero Christoffel symbols. The book prints Gamma^v_xx = 2F'/F and Gamma^v_yy = 2G'/G; direct computation with g^{uv} = -2 gives 2FF' and 2GG'.

key_equations.name: Riemann components of the ansatz
key_equations.meaning: Curvature is controlled by the second derivatives of the profiles.

key_equations.name: Vacuum Einstein equation for the plane wave
key_equations.meaning: Single condition (R_uu = 0) for an exact vacuum plane wave.

key_equations.name: Small-amplitude check
key_equations.meaning: F = 1 + eps, G = 1 - eps satisfies eqn 46.75 to first order, recovering h_xx = -h_yy = eps (+ polarization).

key_equations.name: Interferometer phase shift
key_equations.meaning: Output phase tracks h_+ with sensitivity proportional to arm length; as printed the laser frequency omega_0 (over c) and an overall sign are dropped from Delta phi = omega_0(2 delta y - 2 delta x).

key_equations.name: Equal-arm response
key_equations.meaning: Longer arms mean bigger signal; the linear intensity-phase relation holds only near a chosen operating point.

key_equations.name: Averaged second-order Einstein tensor (Exercise 46.2)
key_equations.meaning: Combined with 46.52 gives eqn 46.53.

key_equations.name: Tensor virial identity (Exercise 46.3)
key_equations.meaning: Key step behind eqn 46.43: the stress integral equals half the second derivative of the second moment.

key_equations.name: TT projection (Exercise 46.5)
key_equations.meaning: Extracts the transverse-traceless part for propagation along n.

key_equations.name: Angular averages
key_equations.meaning: Isotropic integrals used to evaluate the total power.

key_equations.name: Integrated TT square
key_equations.meaning: Multiplying by G/(8 pi c^5) gives G/(5c^5). The reading copy shows T for I.

key_equations.name: Second mass moment of the circular binary (Exercise 46.6)
key_equations.latex: I^{ij} = Ma^2\begin{pmatrix}1 + \cos2\omega t&\sin2\omega t&0\\\sin2\omega t&1 - \cos2\omega t&0\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}
key_equations.meaning: Time dependence at twice the orbital frequency.

key_equations.name: Wave from the binary along the orbital axis
key_equations.meaning: Circularly polarized (+ and x a quarter cycle apart) at twice the orbital frequency.

key_equations.name: Squared third derivative for the binary
key_equations.meaning: Feeds eqn 46.61.

figures.label: Fig. 46.1(a)
figures.caption_paraphrase: The starting configuration: free test masses placed on a circle before any wave arrives.
figures.visual_description: Sixteen small black dots evenly spaced around a thin circle, with the panel letter (a) at upper left. No axes, arrows or labels besides the letter.
figures.what_it_teaches: Sets the reference ring against which the + and x deformations are judged; the wave travels perpendicular to the page.

redesign.idea: A 3D scene: a ring of glowing beads floating in space with a translucent wave front approaching along the axis perpendicular to the ring, so learners see that the wave moves at right angles to the plane where the beads respond.
redesign.interaction: Orbit the camera; press play to send a wave through; a toggle hides the wave front and shows only the beads; a slider adds more concentric rings to show displacement grows with radius.

figures.label: Fig. 46.1(b), upper
figures.caption_paraphrase: Plus polarization at one phase of the cycle: the ring is squeezed horizontally and stretched vertically.
figures.visual_description: Panel (b), upper: the sixteen dots now lie on an upright ellipse, taller than it is wide. From each dot a short thin line runs back toward where that dot sat on the original circle. Top and bottom dots have moved outward, so their lines point toward the centre. Side dots have moved inward, so their lines point away from the centre.
figures.what_it_teaches: Under h_+ free masses move along the x and y axes in antiphase: one axis stretches while the other compresses.

redesign.idea: Phase-dial ring: a single ring of beads animated by h_+ cos(omega t), with a circular phase dial so learners can stop exactly at the moment of maximum vertical stretch and compare with the undeformed circle drawn as a ghost.
redesign.interaction: Drag the phase dial; adjust amplitude with a slider (exaggerated up to 0.3); displacement arrows from ghost to bead update live; readouts of the x and y diameters.

figures.label: Fig. 46.1(b), lower
figures.caption_paraphrase: Plus polarization half a cycle later: the ring is now stretched horizontally and squeezed vertically.
figures.visual_description: Unlettered panel under (b): the dots lie on an ellipse wider than it is tall, the opposite of the panel above. Each dot's short line points back to its place on the original circle. The left and right dots have moved outward and the top and bottom dots inward.
figures.what_it_teaches: The deformation reverses every half period, so the two axes take turns stretching.

redesign.idea: Strip-chart companion to the phase-dial ring: two traces showing the x-diameter and y-diameter versus time, visibly 180 degrees out of step, with a moving cursor linked to the ring animation.
redesign.interaction: Scrub the cursor along the time axis to move the ring; tap either trace to highlight the beads on that axis.

figures.label: Fig. 46.1(c), upper
figures.caption_paraphrase: Cross polarization at one phase: the ring is distorted along a diagonal.
figures.visual_description: Panel letter (c) above an ellipse of dots whose long axis is tilted at 45 degrees to the page edges. Each dot has a short tail line showing its offset from the original circle, so the pattern resembles the (b) ellipse turned through half a right angle.
figures.what_it_teaches: h_x produces the same stretch-and-squeeze but along axes rotated by 45 degrees.
concepts: 45 degree polarization rotation and field rank

redesign.idea: Polarization mixer: one ring driven by h_+ and h_x with independent amplitude and phase sliders, so learners can dial from pure +, through a tilted linear state, to pure x and to circular polarization where the ellipse rotates.
redesign.interaction: Two amplitude sliders and a relative-phase slider; a small inset shows the point (h_+, h_x) tracing a line or circle; a button snaps to the pure x case to match the book panel.

figures.label: Fig. 46.1(c), lower
figures.caption_paraphrase: Cross polarization half a cycle later: the diagonal distortion flips to the other diagonal.
figures.visual_description: An ellipse of dots elongated along the diagonal perpendicular to that of the upper (c) panel, with short tails indicating displacements from the original circle.
figures.what_it_teaches: As with +, the x pattern alternates between two perpendicular orientations, and the pair of x orientations is rotated 45 degrees relative to the + pair.
concepts: 45 degree polarization rotation and field rank

redesign.idea: Rotation-symmetry probe: overlay the + and x rings and let the learner rotate the x pattern with a handle until it matches the + pattern, reading off 45 degrees; then do the same for electromagnetic polarization arrows, which need 90 degrees.
redesign.interaction: Drag a rotation handle; a match indicator lights when patterns coincide; toggle between gravity (spin 2) and light (spin 1) modes.

figures.label: Fig. 46.2(a), upper
figures.caption_paraphrase: Acceleration field lines of a + polarized wave at one instant.
figures.visual_description: Horizontal and vertical axis lines cross at the centre, labelled (a). In each quadrant two curved lines bend around the origin like hyperbolae, approaching the axes asymptotically, with arrowheads showing the direction of relative acceleration: flow comes in along one axis and leaves along the other.
figures.what_it_teaches: The tidal acceleration of free particles has a saddle (quadrupole) shape aligned with the x and y axes for the + polarization.

redesign.idea: Live tidal field: a quiver plot of the acceleration -E_ij x^j computed from h_+ and h_x, with streamlines, animated through the cycle and overlaid on the deforming ring of masses so arrows visibly push beads.
redesign.interaction: Play or scrub phase; toggle streamlines, arrows or ring; move a probe point to see its acceleration vector and its linear growth with distance from the centre.

figures.label: Fig. 46.2(a), lower
figures.caption_paraphrase: The + acceleration field half a cycle later, with every arrow reversed.
figures.visual_description: The same crossed axes and four pairs of hyperbola-like curves as the panel above, but the arrowheads point the opposite way, so the inflow and outflow axes have swapped.
figures.what_it_teaches: The tidal field oscillates in sign at the wave frequency.

redesign.idea: Side-by-side comparison with a quadrupole magnet: the gravitational acceleration field next to the magnetic field of a four-pole magnet, with a slider that morphs one into the other to make the analogy and its limits explicit (the gravitational pattern oscillates and is not sourced by poles).
redesign.interaction: Morph slider; toggle phase flip; hover to show field formula for each panel.

figures.label: Fig. 46.2(b), upper
figures.caption_paraphrase: Acceleration field lines of a x polarized wave at one instant.
figures.visual_description: Crossed horizontal and vertical axes labelled (b), with more closely packed curved field lines that bend around the diagonals rather than the axes, arrowheads on the curves and on the axis ends. The saddle pattern is the (a) pattern turned by 45 degrees.
figures.what_it_teaches: For the x polarization the stretching and squeezing directions lie along the diagonals.

redesign.idea: Eigen-axes overlay: on the live tidal-field plot draw the principal stretch and squeeze axes (eigenvectors of E_ij) as coloured bars whose orientation rotates as the learner mixes + and x.
redesign.interaction: Sliders for h_+ and h_x; eigen-axes and eigenvalue readout update; snap buttons for pure + and pure x.

figures.label: Fig. 46.2(b), lower
figures.caption_paraphrase: The x acceleration field half a cycle later, arrows reversed.
figures.visual_description: Same diagonal-aligned field-line pattern as the panel above with arrowheads pointing the other way.
figures.what_it_teaches: The x tidal field also flips sign every half period.

redesign.idea: Covered by the live tidal-field demo; add a small looping thumbnail showing the four panels of Fig. 46.2 as successive frames so learners connect static panels to the animation.
redesign.interaction: Click a thumbnail to jump the main demo to that polarization and phase.

figures.label: Fig. 46.3
figures.caption_paraphrase: Hulse-Taylor pulsar: measured cumulative shift in periastron time versus year, compared with the general-relativity prediction for gravitational-wave orbital decay.
figures.visual_description: A data plot with horizontal axis Year from 1975 to past 2010 and vertical axis Cumulative shift of periastron time in seconds, running from 0 at the top down to about -65 in steps of 5. A flat horizontal line along the top is labelled Line of Zero Orbital Decay. Black data points fall away from it along a smoothly steepening downward parabola, lying on a solid curve labelled General Relativity Prediction; points are dense in the 1970s-80s and sparser later.
figures.what_it_teaches: Orbital energy loss makes periastron arrive progressively earlier; the accumulated shift grows quadratically in time and matches the quadrupole prediction with no free parameters.
concepts: binary inspiral driven by gravitational radiation

redesign.idea: Orbital-decay laboratory: learners set pulsar masses, orbital period and eccentricity, the app computes dP/dt from the quadrupole formula (with the eccentricity enhancement) and plots the predicted cumulative periastron shift against idealized data points; a switch shows the circular-orbit formula of Example 46.11 underpredicting by about a factor of 12.
redesign.interaction: Sliders for masses, period, eccentricity; checkbox for circular approximation; timeline scrubber showing how the curve accumulates year by year; readout of dP/dt in microseconds per year.

figures.label: Fig. 46.4(a)
figures.visual_description: A plus-shaped layout labelled (a): a hatched rectangle labelled laser at the bottom sends a vertical beam up to a diagonal beam splitter at the centre. One arm runs upward to a round mass (mirror) labelled mass, another runs left to a second mass; small double-headed arrows on both arms show light going out and back. To the right a beam leads to a photodetector labelled detector.
figures.what_it_teaches: A Michelson interferometer whose mirrors are free test masses turns differential arm-length changes into light intensity at the detector.

redesign.idea: Build-an-interferometer: a top-down 2D bench where the learner places laser, beam splitter and end mirrors, sees beam paths animate, and watches the output fringe brightness as one mirror is nudged by fractions of a wavelength.
redesign.interaction: Drag components; nudge a mirror with fine and coarse controls; output intensity meter and phase readout; toggle Fabry-Perot cavities to multiply the effective arm length.

figures.label: Fig. 46.4(b)
figures.caption_paraphrase: One phase of a passing + wave: the ring of test masses is stretched horizontally and the interferometer's horizontal arm lengthens while the vertical arm shortens.
figures.visual_description: Upper-left inset labelled (b): crossed axes with a horizontally elongated ellipse of eight dots. Beside it the interferometer from panel (a) redrawn with the left mass farther from the beam splitter and the top mass closer, with laser, beam splitter and detector labelled.
figures.what_it_teaches: The arm along the stretched direction gets longer and the perpendicular arm shorter, which is exactly what the Michelson geometry is sensitive to.

redesign.idea: Linked views: the deforming ring and the interferometer share one phase slider, arm lengths are drawn with exaggerated strain, and a trace of the output phase is plotted underneath so the learner sees ring shape, arm lengths and signal move together.
redesign.interaction: Phase slider or play; exaggeration factor slider; rotate the detector relative to the wave polarization to see the response fall to zero for a pure x wave aligned with the arms.

figures.label: Fig. 46.4(c)
figures.caption_paraphrase: The opposite phase: ring stretched vertically, horizontal arm shortened and vertical arm lengthened.
figures.visual_description: Inset labelled (c) shows crossed axes with a vertically elongated ellipse of dots; the interferometer beside it has its left mass drawn closer to the beam splitter and its top mass farther away.
figures.what_it_teaches: The arm changes reverse each half cycle, producing an oscillating output.

redesign.idea: Antenna-pattern explorer: a 3D sphere around the detector coloured by response magnitude for + and x waves arriving from each sky direction, with the current (c) configuration shown as a single arrival direction.
redesign.interaction: Rotate the sky sphere; click a direction to launch a wave from there and see the ring and arm responses; toggle polarization angle.

figures.label: Fig. 46.5
figures.caption_paraphrase: The signal GW150914 recorded by the LIGO Hanford and Livingston detectors, raw and reconstructed.
figures.visual_description: Four panels in two columns titled Hanford, Washington (H1) and Livingston, Louisiana (L1). Vertical axes show Strain in units of 1e-21 from -1.0 to 1.0; horizontal axes show Time in seconds from about 0.26 to 0.46. Top row: noisy observed strain (dark line); in the L1 panel the H1 data, shifted and inverted, is overlaid in a lighter line. Bottom row: smooth waveforms labelled Numerical relativity with grey bands for reconstructed wavelet and template fits. Oscillations grow in frequency and amplitude up to a peak near 0.42 s and then die away quickly.
figures.what_it_teaches: A chirp: inspiral frequency and amplitude rise together to merger and then ring down; the same pattern in two widely separated detectors, and agreement with numerical relativity, make the detection convincing.
concepts: binary inspiral driven by gravitational radiation

redesign.idea: Chirp decoder: learners adjust the two component masses and distance, a leading-order chirp (frequency sweeping as the orbit decays under the quadrupole formula) is overlaid on a stylized noisy strain trace, with a play button that also turns the waveform into audio; a second view shows the arrival delay and sign flip between two detectors.
redesign.interaction: Sliders for masses and distance; noise level slider; play audio; drag a time-shift handle between H1 and L1 traces to find the best overlap.

worked_examples.label: Example 46.1
worked_examples.problem: Simplify the sourceless Maxwell equation for the potential by exploiting gauge freedom.
worked_examples.method: Shift to a potential obeying d_mu A^mu = 0, which deletes the divergence term.
worked_examples.key_insight: Gauge choice turns a coupled equation into a plain wave equation for each component.
worked_examples.result: d^2 A^mu = 0 with plane-wave solutions Re[epsilon e^{ik.x}], omega = |k|.

worked_examples.label: Example 46.2
worked_examples.problem: Find the conditions a plane gravitational wave must satisfy in Lorenz gauge.
worked_examples.method: Differentiate the ansatz: the gauge condition gives i k^nu A_{mu nu} = 0 and the wave equation gives -k.k A = 0.
worked_examples.key_insight: Both gauge and field equation become algebra on the amplitude; nontrivial waves need null k.
concepts: null wavevector and propagation at the speed of light

worked_examples.label: Example 46.3
worked_examples.problem: Determine how an oscillatory residual gauge transformation changes the wave amplitude.
worked_examples.method: Take xi_alpha = B_alpha e^{ik.x}, apply the linearized transformation to h, trace-reverse, and substitute.
worked_examples.key_insight: The amplitude shifts by combinations of B and k, and transversality survives, so B is free to impose further conditions.
worked_examples.result: A' = A - i(B_alpha k_beta + B_beta k_alpha - eta_{alpha beta} B.k) (eqn 46.19).
concepts: residual gauge transformation in linearized gravity

worked_examples.label: Example 46.4
worked_examples.problem: Write the TT-gauge amplitude and line element for a wave travelling along z, seen by an observer at rest.
worked_examples.method: Use A u = 0 with u = (1,0,0,0) to kill time components, transversality with k along z to kill z components, tracelessness for A_yy = -A_xx and symmetry for A_yx = A_xy.
worked_examples.key_insight: Only two numbers survive; the metric shows oscillating transverse distances, and setting either number to zero gives two waves related by 45 degrees.

worked_examples.label: Example 46.5
worked_examples.problem: Does a single test mass at rest move when the wave passes?
worked_examples.method: Geodesic equation for a mass at rest reduces to x-double-dot = -Gamma^i_00, which vanishes because h_0a = 0 in TT gauge.
worked_examples.key_insight: The coordinate position is frozen, which says nothing physical: TT coordinates are tied to free masses.
worked_examples.result: Coordinate acceleration zero (eqn 46.25); resolved afterwards by the proper-distance integral 46.26.
concepts: TT coordinates of free test masses

worked_examples.label: Example 46.6
worked_examples.problem: Find the relative motion of two free masses initially separated along x by a small distance a.
worked_examples.method: Specialize geodesic deviation to R^mu_{0 alpha 0}, compute the needed linearized Riemann components from h, replace tau by t to first order, and read off second-order ODEs; repeat for a y separation.
worked_examples.key_insight: Relative acceleration equals half the separation times the second time derivative of the strain, so integrating twice gives displacement linear in h.
worked_examples.result: n^i = (1/2) h^TT_ij x^j (eqn 46.33) with h_+ and h_x identified.

worked_examples.label: Example 46.7
worked_examples.problem: Express the tidal effect of the wave as a tensor decomposed into polarizations.
worked_examples.method: Define E_ij = R_0i0j, use the TT Riemann components, and expand on tensor-product bases.
worked_examples.key_insight: The wave's tidal field is just minus half the second derivative of h^TT, split cleanly onto e_+ and e_x.
worked_examples.result: E = -(1/2)(ddot h_+ e_+ + ddot h_x e_x) with e_+ and e_x in 46.35-46.36.

worked_examples.label: Example 46.8
worked_examples.problem: Which multipoles of a source can emit electromagnetic and gravitational radiation?
worked_examples.method: List multipole moments; ask which are fixed by conservation laws (charge; mass, momentum, angular momentum); use metric expansions and dimensional scaling of mass and current moments.
worked_examples.key_insight: Conservation laws, not dynamics, forbid monopole and dipole gravitational radiation, so the mass quadrupole leads.
worked_examples.result: Lowest gravitational radiation is quadrupolar; current moments are suppressed by v.
concepts: absence of monopole and dipole gravitational radiation

worked_examples.label: Example 46.9
worked_examples.problem: Estimate the strain at Earth from two 30 solar-mass black holes orbiting at 10 Hz with separation 2000 km, 100 Mpc away.
worked_examples.method: Insert ddot I ~ 4 M a^2 omega^2 into the quadrupole formula with c restored.
worked_examples.key_insight: Even an extreme source gives strain of a few parts in 1e21.
worked_examples.result: |hbar| ~ 32 pi^2 G M a^2 f^2/(c^4 R) ~ 5e-21 (eqn 46.46). Own check: with a = 1000 km the arithmetic gives 5.0e-21; Kepler's law for these masses gives an orbital frequency near 5 Hz, so 10 Hz is best read as the wave frequency.

worked_examples.label: Example 46.10
worked_examples.problem: Estimate the gravitational luminosity of the same binary and the flux at Earth.
worked_examples.method: Use <dddot I dddot I> = 128 M^2 a^4 omega^6 (Exercise 46.6) in the quadrupole luminosity.
worked_examples.key_insight: Enormous total power but tiny flux at cosmological distance; the omega^6 dependence favours tight, fast orbits.
worked_examples.result: L ~ 1e47 W (eqn 46.61); flux about a milliwatt per square metre (own recomputation with the book's inputs: L ~ 1.5e47 W, flux ~ 1.3 mW m^-2).

worked_examples.label: Example 46.11
worked_examples.problem: How fast does the orbital period of an equal-mass circular binary decay because of gravitational radiation?
worked_examples.method: Newtonian orbit: force balance gives omega; virial energy E = -GM^2/(4a); express L and E in terms of a and P; differentiate E proportional to P^{-2/3}.
worked_examples.key_insight: Because E is negative, losing energy shortens the period: radiation speeds the orbit up.
concepts: binary inspiral driven by gravitational radiation

worked_examples.label: Example 46.12
worked_examples.problem: Show that the full nonlinear Einstein equation admits plane-wave solutions.
worked_examples.method: Take ds^2 = -du dv + F(u)^2 dx^2 + G(u)^2 dy^2, compute connections and Riemann components, impose vacuum, test F = 1 + eps, G = 1 - eps.
worked_examples.key_insight: The vacuum equations collapse to one ODE linking F and G; its small-amplitude limit is the linearized + wave.
worked_examples.result: F''/F + G''/G = 0 (eqn 46.75), satisfied to first order by F = 1 + eps, G = 1 - eps.

worked_examples.label: Example 46.13
worked_examples.problem: Relate the interferometer output to the wave amplitude.
worked_examples.method: Phase difference from round-trip arm-length changes, with displacements from eqn 46.33.
worked_examples.key_insight: Signal is proportional to arm length times strain, so long arms are essential.
worked_examples.result: Delta phi = (L_x + L_y) h_+ and I proportional to 2 L h_+ (eqns 46.77-46.78), with omega_0/c and sign suppressed.

worked_examples.problem: Margin note 9: show that a gravitational plane wave travels at the speed of light.
worked_examples.method: Follow a photon along x = k lambda + l with null k and dot with k_mu.
worked_examples.key_insight: The wave phase is constant along a light ray, so photon and wave move in lockstep.
concepts: null wavevector and propagation at the speed of light

worked_examples.problem: Compute the physical distance between two free masses on the x axis as a + wave passes.
worked_examples.method: Integrate sqrt(g_xx) along x, take the real part and expand the square root to first order.
worked_examples.key_insight: What oscillates is proper distance, even though coordinates do not.

worked_examples.problem: Derive the total power radiated in gravitational waves by a slowly moving source.
worked_examples.method: Energy density from the TT Isaacson tensor plus quadrupole formula; flux through a sphere via energy conservation and the divergence theorem; outgoing-wave relation t^{0r} = t^{00}; TT identity and isotropic angular integrals.
worked_examples.key_insight: The direction-dependent TT projection averages over the sky to a fixed fraction (2/5 of the naive sum) of the full quadrupole squared.
concepts: energy flux through a distant sphere

worked_examples.problem: Check that angular momentum lost by the binary equals that carried by the waves.
worked_examples.method: Evaluate eqn 46.63 with the binary's quadrupole (Exercise 46.7); independently write E in terms of J and use dJ/dt = -(J/2E) dE/dt.
worked_examples.key_insight: Two routes agree, and dJ/dt = L/omega as required for circular orbits.
worked_examples.result: |dJ/dt| = 4 G^{7/2} M^{9/2}/(5 a^{7/2} c^5) (eqns 46.69-46.70). The printed J = sqrt(G M a^3) = -E omega/2 should read sqrt(G M^3 a) = -2E/omega.
concepts: angular momentum carried by gravitational waves
binary inspiral driven by gravitational radiation

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Gravity as a second gauge field: every step for electromagnetic waves repeated with one more index
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: linearized vacuum wave equation for hbar
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Section 46.1 walks through Lorenz gauge, plane waves, residual gauge and transversality for A_mu, then reruns the same argument for hbar_{mu nu}; polarization vectors become polarization matrices.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Gravity's gauge freedom is a coordinate change with a vector parameter, the field is symmetric rank-2, and gravity is nonlinear because the waves carry energy; there is no gravitational analogue of opposite charges, which changes the radiation selection rules.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Split-screen derivation where each EM line has a gravity twin; learners click a line to see which object gained an index and why.

analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: TT coordinates of free test masses
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Raised as the naive expectation for how suspended masses respond, then shown to be misleading: coordinates stay put and the real effect is transverse relative stretching.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Water waves displace floats vertically (along the gradient of a potential); gravitational waves have no single-particle displacement and act only on separations, perpendicular to travel.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Contrast animation: bobbing boats on a water wave next to a ring of beads in a gravitational wave, with a single bead highlighted to show it has no absolute motion.

analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: The acceleration field lines of Fig. 46.2 are compared with the field of a four-pole magnet, setting up the question of quadrupole sources.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The magnet field is static and sourced by poles at the corners; the gravitational tidal pattern oscillates in time and is a property of the passing wave, not of nearby sources.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Morph slider between a quadrupole magnet's field and the tidal field of a + wave.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Radio transmitter as an oscillating dipole
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: absence of monopole and dipole gravitational radiation
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Antennas radiate by driving charge back and forth; the gravitational analogue fails because the centre of mass cannot oscillate for an isolated system, so gravity must shake a quadrupole.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Mass has one sign, so there is no way to build a gravitational dipole oscillator; the analogy works by showing where it breaks.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Toy sources: drag charges or masses; a meter shows which moments oscillate and a far-field panel shows radiation appearing only for allowed moments.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: A photon surfing with the gravitational wave
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: null wavevector and propagation at the speed of light
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: A light ray moving along k keeps a constant phase of the gravitational wave, so the two travel together.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Shows consistency of the phase fronts with light rays for a plane wave in flat background; says nothing about dispersion or propagation through curved backgrounds.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Spacetime diagram with wave-crest lines and a photon worldline that stays on one crest.

analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Photons carry no charge, so light does not source more electromagnetism in vacuum; gravitational waves carry energy, which is the 'charge' of gravity, so they gravitate and the theory is nonlinear.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Energy of gravitational waves is only defined after averaging, unlike electric charge which is local.

analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: The detector is the same interferometer geometry that tested the ether, but with arms of kilometres rather than about a metre, and extended further by optical cavities.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Michelson-Morley compared light speeds along rigid arms; LIGO measures time-varying proper-length changes between free mirrors.

analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Millisecond pulsars tick so regularly that tiny timing residuals reveal passing low-frequency waves, and a binary pulsar's clock reveals its orbital decay.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Timing residuals mix wave effects with spin-down, dispersion and noise; years of data are needed.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Pulse train with arrival-time residuals plotted as a slow gravitational wave passes between pulsar and Earth.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A passing gravitational wave makes each free mass bob back and forth, like a boat on the sea.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: No single free mass has a measurable absolute motion; in TT coordinates it keeps fixed coordinates, and the physical effect is an oscillation of distances between masses, transverse to propagation.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Everyday waves (water, sound) move matter at each point, and the line element visibly oscillates.
concepts: TT coordinates of free test masses

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: If the geodesic equation gives zero coordinate acceleration, the wave has no physical effect.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Coordinates in a chosen gauge carry no physical meaning; the invariant proper distance between masses oscillates and geodesic deviation gives nonzero tidal accelerations.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: In Newtonian physics and in simple frames, coordinate acceleration equals physical acceleration.
concepts: TT coordinates of free test masses

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The two gravitational polarizations are perpendicular, like x and y polarized light.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The + and x patterns are related by a 45 degree rotation; rotating by 90 degrees turns a + wave into minus itself.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Linear polarizations of light are 90 degrees apart, and the chapter builds explicitly on that analogy.
concepts: 45 degree polarization rotation and field rank

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Gravitational radiation, like electromagnetic radiation, can come from an oscillating dipole.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Momentum conservation fixes the mass dipole and angular-momentum conservation fixes the current dipole; the leading radiation is quadrupolar.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Dipole antennas are the textbook radiators and gravity and electromagnetism share inverse-square laws.
concepts: absence of monopole and dipole gravitational radiation

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Any rotating or pulsating massive body emits gravitational waves.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Only a time-varying quadrupole radiates; a spherically symmetric star, even if spinning or pulsating radially, emits none, and an axisymmetric rotator emits no angular momentum.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Motion of mass feels like it should disturb the field, and accelerating charges always seem to radiate.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Gravitational field energy has a definite density at each point, like electromagnetic energy.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: In a freely falling frame gravity vanishes locally, so the energy of gravitational waves is meaningful only after averaging over several wavelengths and periods.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Electromagnetic energy density E^2 + B^2 is local, and waves obviously carry energy.
concepts: effective energy-momentum tensor of gravitational waves

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A binary that loses energy slows down and drifts apart.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Bound orbits have negative total energy; losing energy makes it more negative, the orbit shrinks and the stars speed up, so the period decreases.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: In daily life losing energy means slowing down (friction), and kinetic energy is positive.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Gravitational waves are an artefact of linearizing Einstein's equation.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Exact plane-wave solutions of the full vacuum equation exist and reduce to the linear waves at small amplitude.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The chapter derives everything in the linear approximation and admits gravity is nonlinear.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The + and x polarizations differ by a 45 degree phase in time.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: They are two independent spatial patterns related by a 45 degree rotation; their temporal phase relation is free (a quarter-cycle offset gives circular polarization).
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The chapter summary itself uses the phrase 'out of phase' for the rotation.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The I_ij in the quadrupole formula is the rigid-body moment of inertia tensor from mechanics.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: It is the second mass moment, the integral of rho y_i y_j; the mechanics tensor is the integral of rho(r^2 delta_ij - y_i y_j). They differ by sign and a trace term.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The book calls it the moment of inertia tensor.
concepts: second mass moment and reduced quadrupole moment

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Gravitational waves are longitudinal compressions like sound waves.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: They are transverse: in TT gauge nothing happens along the propagation direction, and the stretching occurs in the perpendicular plane.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A detector responds equally to waves from every direction and polarization.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: An L-shaped interferometer measures the difference of strains along its arms, so its response depends on the arrival direction and polarization angle and can vanish (for example a x wave aligned with the arms from overhead).
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The chapter only treats a + wave arriving perpendicular to the detector plane.

thought_experiments.name: Ring of free test masses
thought_experiments.setup: A circle of freely floating masses in the plane transverse to an incoming plane gravitational wave.
thought_experiments.lesson: The ring deforms into oscillating ellipses (+ along the axes, x along the diagonals), making polarization tangible and showing displacements grow with distance from the centre.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Draggable rings of different radii and orientations; measure diameters as the wave passes.

thought_experiments.name: The mass that refuses to move
thought_experiments.setup: A single test mass at rest at the origin in TT coordinates while a wave passes.
thought_experiments.lesson: Its coordinates never change, forcing the move from coordinate positions to invariant distances between two masses.
concepts: TT coordinates of free test masses
thought_experiments.app_idea: Coordinate grid that stretches with the wave so a bead stays on its grid point while a ruler between beads visibly changes length.

thought_experiments.name: Photon riding a wave crest
thought_experiments.setup: A photon launched along the wavevector of a gravitational plane wave.
thought_experiments.lesson: It stays on a surface of constant wave phase forever, so the wave moves at the speed of light.
concepts: null wavevector and propagation at the speed of light

thought_experiments.name: Trying to make a monopole radiate
thought_experiments.setup: Imagine making the total charge (or total mass) of a bounded object oscillate to produce spherical waves.
thought_experiments.lesson: Conservation laws forbid it; for gravity the dipole is frozen as well, leaving the quadrupole as the first radiator.
concepts: absence of monopole and dipole gravitational radiation
thought_experiments.app_idea: Attempt-to-radiate sandbox where forbidden moves are blocked with a message naming the conservation law.

thought_experiments.name: Shaking a fist in anger
thought_experiments.setup: Exercise 46.4 asks for the gravitational power radiated by the solar system, a black-hole binary, and a shaken fist, using P ~ G^4 m^5/(r^5 c^5).
thought_experiments.lesson: Everyday and planetary sources radiate absurdly little because of the G/c^5 prefactor; only compact relativistic systems matter.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Log-scale power ladder from a waving hand to merging black holes with a slider for mass, size and speed.

historical_notes.event: Suggested that gravitational disturbances propagate as waves. The book names him but gives no date; 1905 comes from outside the book.
historical_notes.significance: Anticipated gravitational waves before general relativity existed.

historical_notes.event: Predicted gravitational waves from linearized general relativity (the book prints 1906); the quadrupole formula followed in 1918.
historical_notes.significance: Theoretical origin of the chapter's central result.

historical_notes.event: Discovered the binary pulsar PSR B1913+16, whose measured orbital decay later matched the gravitational-wave prediction; Nobel Prize 1993.
historical_notes.significance: First, indirect, evidence that gravitational waves carry energy away.

historical_notes.event: Direct detection of GW150914 from a binary black-hole merger by both LIGO detectors on 14 September 2015; Nobel Prize 2017.
historical_notes.significance: Opened gravitational-wave astronomy and provided strong-field tests of general relativity.

historical_notes.event: Margin note 24: the Michelson-Morley null result tested a v^2/c^2 ether effect predicted by Lorentz and led him to propose length contraction; its interferometer geometry is reused by LIGO.
historical_notes.significance: Links the oldest precision interferometry in relativity to modern detectors, and notes it was not central to Einstein's motivation.

applications_and_observations.topic: Strain from a stellar-mass black-hole binary
applications_and_observations.details: Quadrupole formula applied to two 30 solar-mass black holes 100 Mpc away.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: M = 30 M_sun each, 2a = 2000 km, f = 10 Hz, R = 100 Mpc gives |h| ~ 5e-21.

applications_and_observations.topic: Static potential of the Earth versus wave strain
applications_and_observations.details: Compares the wave amplitude with the Newtonian metric perturbation at the Earth's surface to motivate a background-plus-ripple split.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: |h_00| = 2GM_E/(R_E c^2) ~ 1e-9 versus h ~ 1e-21; detected frequencies tens of Hz to kHz, wavelengths tens to thousands of km.

applications_and_observations.details: Quadrupole luminosity for the same system; L grows as omega^6.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: L ~ 1e47 W; flux at Earth under about 1 mW m^-2 (own recomputation: 1.5e47 W and 1.3 mW m^-2 with the book's inputs).

applications_and_observations.details: Radio pulses from one neutron star time the orbit; the orbital period shrinks as predicted, shown as cumulative periastron-time shift in Fig. 46.3.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Pulsar period 59 ms; orbital period about 7.75 h; period decrease about 76.5 microseconds per year. Own estimate: the circular equal-mass formula (46.68) with M = 1.4 M_sun gives dP/dt ~ -2e-13, about 12 times smaller than observed (-2.4e-12), the difference being the eccentricity (e ~ 0.62) enhancement.

applications_and_observations.details: Two L-shaped detectors in Hanford, Washington and Livingston, Louisiana with Fabry-Perot arm cavities; light must stay in the arms for about half a wave period.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Band about 10 Hz to 10 kHz; arms given as 4.2 km (actual LIGO arms are 4 km); effective optical length ~1200 km; fractional displacement ~1e-21; Michelson-Morley arms ~1.3 m.

applications_and_observations.details: Binary black-hole inspiral, merger and ringdown seen by both LIGO detectors; Fig. 46.5 shows the strain traces and numerical-relativity fits.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: 14 September 2015, 09:50:45 UTC; masses ~36 and 29 M_sun; remnant ~62 M_sun; ~3 M_sun c^2 radiated; peak strain ~1e-21.

applications_and_observations.details: Einstein Telescope and Cosmic Explorer are planned to improve sensitivity about tenfold and reach compact objects in the early Universe.
Proposed space interferometer for low-frequency waves from seed, intermediate-mass and lighter supermassive black-hole binaries at high redshift.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Band ~100 microHz to 100 mHz; masses 1e2 to 1e7 M_sun.

applications_and_observations.details: Arrival times of pulses from many millisecond pulsars are monitored for years; a wave perturbs timing through its effect at the pulsar and at Earth.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Band nanohertz to microhertz; sources are supermassive black-hole binaries.

applications_and_observations.details: Relic waves from the Big Bang expected to dominate the spectrum at the lowest frequencies; whether any part is detectable depends on the cosmological model.

applications_and_observations.topic: Gravitational power of everyday and solar-system sources
applications_and_observations.details: Exercise 46.4 sets up the estimate P ~ G^4 m^5/(r^5 c^5) for the solar system, a black-hole binary and a shaken fist.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Own estimate: Sun-Jupiter radiates about 5 kW; Sun-Earth about 200 W; a waved arm far below 1e-40 W.

notation_and_conventions.convention: eta = diag(-1, 1, 1, 1); geometrized units G = c = 1 for most derivations, with G and c restored in quadrupole, power and numerical results.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Mixed use: eqn 46.68 lacks the 1/c^5 needed in SI; eqns 46.42-46.44 use t - R for t - R/c.

notation_and_conventions.convention: k.x means k_mu x^mu, so e^{ik.x} = e^{-i(omega t - |k| z)} for a wave along z; Re[ ] is understood and often dropped.
hbar_{mu nu} = h_{mu nu} - (1/2) eta_{mu nu} h; in TT gauge hbar = h.
notation_and_conventions.notes: The chapter sometimes switches between h and hbar without comment once in TT gauge.

notation_and_conventions.convention: A coordinate shift by +xi subtracts the symmetrized gradient of xi from the metric perturbation (eqn 46.17), and trace reversal adds an eta times divergence term (eqn 46.18).
notation_and_conventions.notes: Some texts use the opposite sign for xi.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Commas denote partial derivatives; d^2 = eta^{mu nu} d_mu d_nu is the d'Alembertian, so the sourced equation reads -d^2 hbar = 16 pi G T.
h^TT_xx = -h^TT_yy = h_+, h^TT_xy = h^TT_yx = h_x for a wave along z; basis tensors e_+ and e_x.

notation_and_conventions.notes: Same object often called the electric part of the Weyl tensor in other texts.

notation_and_conventions.convention: The linearized Riemann tensor is half an alternating sum of four second derivatives of h (eqn 46.29, taken from Chapter 45), and geodesic deviation for particles at rest carries an explicit minus sign in front of the R^mu_{0 alpha 0} contraction (eqn 46.28), so that R_{x0x0} = -(1/2) times the second time derivative of h_xx.
I_ij denotes the integral of rho y_i y_j (called the moment of inertia tensor); Q_ij its traceless part; dots are time derivatives, three dots in the power formula.
notation_and_conventions.notes: The reading copy frequently drops the third dot.

notation_and_conventions.convention: For purely spatial tensors indices are all written down and repeated indices are summed (margin note 17).
Angle brackets denote averaging over several wavelengths and periods.
Lower-case t_{mu nu} for the effective energy-momentum of gravitational waves, capital T_{mu nu} for matter.
u = t - z, v = t + z with ds^2 = -du dv + dx^2 + dy^2.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Some texts include a factor 1/sqrt(2) or define u = (t - z)/2.

margin_notes.summary: Expands the acronym LIGO.
Gives the Maxwell equation for the potential with a current source on the right.
Explains the shorthand k.x and dropping the prime on the gauge-fixed potential.
Recalls why Lorenz gauge leaves freedom: shifting by the gradient of a function obeying the wave equation preserves the condition.
Notes that omega/|k| = 1 means omega/|k| = c in SI units.
Polarization vectors encode photon spin states; quantum treatment deferred to the next chapter.
Reminder of the sourced linearized equation -d^2 hbar = 16 pi T, to be used again in Section 46.3.
From here on the doubly gauge-fixed potential is written without primes, and taking the real part of wave expressions is left implicit.
Photon-along-k argument showing the gravitational wave phase is constant along a light ray, so the wave moves at c (recovered from the page render; missing in the reading copy).
Points out the electromagnetic residual gauge condition d^2 xi = 0 and that gravity simply adds an index (recovered from the page render).
The 45 degree relation between polarizations was already visible in Example 46.4.
Electromagnetic retarded potential solution of -d^2 A = mu_0 J, which the gravitational solution copies; repeats the argument of eqn 45.31.
Quadrupole formula with factors of c restored.
Points to Exercise 46.3 for the conservation-law step that turns the stress integral into the second moment of the energy density.
Gravitational field energy has no local meaning because free fall removes gravity locally, so gauge dependence of the quadratic term is expected.
The tedious derivation of t_{mu nu} is laid out in Exercise 46.2.
Explains writing all spatial indices downstairs with summation still implied.
Identifies the flux integral as energy carried by the waves, the source losing the same amount (Exercise 46.5).
A spherically symmetric source has constant second moment and so cannot radiate gravitational waves.
The TT contraction identity used in the power calculation is proved in Exercise 46.5(d).
Most orbiting systems radiate negligibly (Exercise 46.4); the example deliberately picks black holes for drama; luminosity scales as omega^6.
Angular-momentum radiation formula taken from Maggiore section 3.3.3; axisymmetric sources lose no angular momentum.
The binary's angular-momentum loss rate is derived in Exercise 46.7.

Biography of Michelson with dates misprinted as 1952-1931; Michelson-Morley tested Lorentz's v^2/c^2 ether correction, prompted length contraction, and was not a main motivation for Einstein; recommends Cheng.
Recommends the 2018 Nobel lectures of Weiss, Barish and Thorne in Reviews of Modern Physics for the LIGO story.

notable.summary: Guided multi-part derivation of the averaged second-order Einstein tensor: expand the Ricci tensor to quadratic order, group thirteen terms, eliminate most using tracelessness, the gauge condition, vanishing averaged divergences and the wave equation, and show the Ricci scalar vanishes.
notable.why_notable: Supplies the otherwise quoted result t_{mu nu} = (c^4/32 pi G)<d h d h> and shows why averaging is essential.

notable.summary: From d_mu T^{mu nu} = 0, derive identities relating time derivatives of the moments of T^00 to spatial stresses, integrate over the source and prove the conservation-law step behind the quadrupole formula.
skills: integration by parts over compact sources
notable.why_notable: Fills the key gap between eqn 46.42 and 46.43; the tensor virial theorem is reusable.

notable.summary: Use Newtonian scalings of velocity and acceleration to estimate wave amplitude, energy density and radiated power, then apply to the solar system, a black-hole binary and a shaken fist.
notable.why_notable: Builds intuition for why only compact relativistic systems are detectable; the fist example is memorable.

notable.summary: Construct the transverse projector for a direction n, show a naive double projection is not traceless, build the TT projector, derive the contraction identity for traceless tensors and evaluate isotropic angular integrals to obtain the 24 pi/15 factor.
notable.why_notable: Provides the machinery that converts eqn 46.58 into the quadrupole luminosity 46.60.

notable.summary: For two equal masses on a circular orbit, find the orbital frequency, the second mass moment, the wave field along the orbital axis at twice the orbital frequency, and the averaged square of the third derivative of the moment.
skills: applying the quadrupole formula to a concrete source
notable.why_notable: Shows the frequency doubling and circular polarization along the axis, and feeds Examples 46.10-46.11.

notable.summary: Using the binary moments, evaluate the angular-momentum radiation formula to reproduce the loss rate quoted in the chapter.
skills: consistency checks between energy and angular momentum loss
notable.why_notable: Confirms dJ/dt = L/omega for circular orbits.

difficulty.notes: The EM-first framing and ring-of-masses pictures are friendly, and the numerical estimates are accessible. The TT gauge construction and geodesic-deviation algebra need solid index skills; the energy-flux section quotes the Isaacson tensor and relies on two long exercises; Section 46.5 needs connection and curvature computation in null coordinates. Several printed slips (eqn 46.24 missing terms, J formula, Gamma^v_xx, dropped c factors and signs in 46.68 and 46.77, historical dates) and OCR losses of dots in the reading copy can confuse a careful reader.

teaching_gems.gem: Teach gravitational waves as a replay of electromagnetic waves: same gauge-fixing sequence, same plane-wave algebra, with each vector becoming a symmetric matrix.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Learners reuse a derivation they already trust and can locate exactly where gravity differs (extra index, 45 degree polarization, quadrupole sources, nonlinearity).
teaching_gems.app_idea: Two-column stepper: EM step on the left, gravity step on the right, with differences highlighted and a counter tracking independent components (4 -> 2 for EM, 10 -> 2 for gravity).

teaching_gems.gem: Stage the 'the mass does not move' paradox before revealing proper distance.
teaching_gems.why_effective: A productive failure makes the gauge meaning of coordinates memorable and motivates geodesic deviation as the invariant tool.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Prediction prompt: learner guesses how a single bead moves, sees its fixed TT coordinates, then drags a ruler to a second bead and watches the length oscillate.

teaching_gems.gem: Ring of free masses as the definition of polarization.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Turns abstract amplitude matrices into shapes; the 45 degree relation and the linear growth of displacement with distance are visible at a glance.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Polarization mixer with h_+ and h_x sliders and relative phase, showing linear and circular polarization of the ring.

teaching_gems.gem: Conservation laws as radiation selection rules: charge kills EM monopole; mass, momentum and angular momentum kill gravitational monopole and both dipoles.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Explains why gravitational radiation is so weak and quadrupolar without solving the multipole problem in full.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Source sandbox with moment meters (I_0, I_1, S_1, I_2) that stay frozen or oscillate as the learner moves masses, with the radiated power readout lighting only for I_2.

teaching_gems.gem: Put numbers in immediately: 5e-21 strain, 1e47 W, milliwatts per square metre, compared with Earth's 1e-9 potential.
teaching_gems.why_effective: The scale shock explains decades of detector development and justifies the background-plus-ripple approximation.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Strain calculator with sliders for masses, separation, frequency and distance, and a comparison bar showing proton widths over the LIGO arm.

teaching_gems.gem: Negative energy makes radiating orbits speed up, linking a one-line energy argument to the Hulse-Taylor data.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Resolves a strong everyday intuition and connects theory to a Nobel-winning measurement.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Energy-well animation: a binary sliding deeper into its potential well as it radiates, with speed and period gauges and a live cumulative periastron-shift plot.

teaching_gems.gem: Photon on a wave crest proves c-propagation in two lines.
teaching_gems.why_effective: A geometric picture replaces an abstract dispersion relation and ties k.k = 0 to light rays.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Spacetime diagram with draggable wave crests and a photon worldline locked to a crest.

teaching_gems.gem: Exact plane wave in null coordinates reduces the full Einstein equation to one ODE.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Offers a rare nonlinear calculation small enough to do by hand, reassuring learners that waves are not an approximation artefact.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Profile designer: sketch F(u), the app integrates G'' = -(F''/F) G numerically and shows free particles focusing, including where the Rosen coordinates break down.

teaching_gems.gem: Detector sensitivity argument: strain is fractional, so the signal scales with arm length and photon storage time must match the wave period.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Explains in plain terms why LIGO is kilometres long and uses optical cavities.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Arm-length slider from 1 m to 1000 km showing phase signal against a fixed noise floor, with a cavity-bounce counter.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Historical slips: Einstein's prediction dated 1906 instead of 1916, Michelson's birth year printed as 1952, spin-up said to be observed in 1974 (the pulsar was found then; decay was reported around 1978-79), and LIGO's arms given as 4.2 km (they are 4 km).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may repeat wrong dates or numbers.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Correct silently in app text; if quoting, use 1916 (and 1918 for the quadrupole formula), 1852-1931, 1974 discovery and 1979 decay measurement, 4 km arms.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Printed eqn 46.24 (pure x wave) omits the dx^2 + dy^2 terms.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Suggests the x wave removes transverse distances entirely, contradicting the 45 degree rotation claim.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Show ds^2 = -dt^2 + dx^2 + dy^2 + 2 h_x dx dy + dz^2 and verify the rotation explicitly.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Eqn 46.15 sets hbar_{mu z} = 0 before TT gauge; Lorenz gauge alone only gives A_{alpha z} = -A_{alpha 0}.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Blurs which conditions come from gauge fixing and which from the field equations.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Track constraints explicitly: Lorenz (4), residual gauge (4), leaving 2; show A_{alpha z} = 0 only after A_{alpha 0} = 0.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Eqn 46.33 writes n^i for what is the change in separation, and the integration step silently drops constants and assumes separations much smaller than the wavelength.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Confusion between total separation and displacement; misapplication to detectors longer than a wavelength.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Write delta x^i = (1/2) h_ij x^j and state the long-wavelength assumption.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The quadrupole formula gives hbar_ij, not its TT part; the text says TT gauge makes the trace irrelevant without mentioning the transverse projection that is only introduced in Exercise 46.5.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may use non-transverse components (e.g. along the line of sight) as physical strain.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Introduce the TT projector Lambda_{ij,kl}(n) alongside eqn 46.44 and show the binary example viewed edge-on and face-on.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: I_ij is called the moment of inertia tensor, and the Q_ij formula omits delta_ij; the luminosity derivation needs a traceless tensor but uses I_ij.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Confusion with the mechanics inertia tensor and errors for sources whose trace varies (e.g. radial pulsation of a non-spherical body).
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Use the reduced quadrupole Q_ij throughout the power formula and note it equals I_ij when Tr I is constant.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Example 46.9 inputs are not mutually consistent: two 30 solar-mass holes at 2000 km separation orbit at about 5 Hz, so the quoted 10 Hz is really the wave frequency; with the book's numbers the flux at Earth is about 1.3 mW m^-2, not below 1 (own calculation).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Careful learners checking with Kepler's law get a mismatch and lose trust.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Present orbital and wave frequency separately (f_GW = 2 f_orb) and recompute; use the discrepancy as a teaching moment.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Sign bookkeeping in Example 46.11 and eqn 46.70: L is defined as dE/dt (positive radiated power) but then used as the orbital energy change, and dP/dt picks up its minus sign only if dE_orb/dt = -L.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Sign errors when deriving decay rates independently.

tutor_notes: Open by asking: 'If gravity propagates at a finite speed, what should happen far away when two stars orbit each other?' Then ask what the learner remembers about how light waves come out of Maxwell's equations.

Order of explanation: EM wave recap -> gravity wave equation -> plane-wave constraints -> TT gauge and the two polarizations -> test masses and geodesic deviation -> ring pictures -> why quadrupole -> quadrupole formula and numbers -> energy and luminosity -> binary inspiral and Hulse-Taylor -> exact plane wave -> detectors and GW150914.
For novices, skip the gauge algebra and start from the ring of masses and the displacement formula delta x = (1/2) h x; return to TT gauge only when they ask why there are exactly two polarizations.
Check understanding: ask the learner to sketch the ring for a + wave, then rotate the sketch by 45 and by 90 degrees and say what polarization each corresponds to.
Check understanding: 'A single free mass in TT coordinates does not move. Does that mean LIGO cannot work?' Look for an answer about distances between masses.
Check understanding: ask why a perfectly spherical star collapsing or pulsating radially emits no gravitational waves, expecting a conservation or symmetry argument about the quadrupole.

Common question: 'If waves stretch space, why don't the laser wavelengths stretch too and cancel the effect?' Answer: light in the arms is affected, but the measurement compares round-trip times in two arms whose storage time is a significant part of the wave period; the effect does not cancel for gravitational-wave frequencies well below the inverse light travel time.

Common question: 'Where does the energy of the waves live?' Emphasize that it cannot be pinned to a point; only averages over many wavelengths make sense, which is also why t_{mu nu} is not a normal tensor field.

Use the numbers: have the learner compute h ~ 1e-21 and turn it into an arm-length change dL = (1/2) h L for a 4 km arm, which is about 2e-18 m. That is roughly 1/400 of a proton radius, so thinking of it as 'a thousandth of a proton' is only the right order of magnitude.
When discussing inspiral, ask the learner to predict whether the orbit speeds up or slows down before showing E = -GM^2/(4a); many will say slows down.
Flag the printed errors (eqn 46.24, J formula, Gamma^v_xx, 46.68 c^5, 46.77 factors, dates) proactively if the learner is working from the book.

Advanced learners: connect the 45 degree rotation to spin 2 (patterns repeat under rotation by 180/s degrees) and preview gravitons; mention circular polarization along the axis of a binary from eqn 46.104.
If the learner asks about eccentric orbits or Hulse-Taylor numbers, introduce the eccentricity enhancement factor rather than letting the circular formula be taken as exact.
